By the KING,

a proclamation,

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGE R.

WHereas We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now Hands prorogued to Tuesday the Fifth Day of July next: We do, for that End, publish this Our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting and Attendance on

Tuesday the said Fifth Day of July next. And We be ing desirous and resolved, as soon as may be, to meet Our People, and to have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known, to all Our loving Subjects, Our Royal Will and Pleasure to call a New Parliament: And do hereby further declare. That, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, We have, this Day, given Order to Our Chancellor of Great Britain to issue out Writs, in due Form, for calling a New Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste on Saturday the Twenty-first Day of this Instant May, and to be returnable on Tuesday the Twelfth Day of July following.

Given at Our Court at Saint , the Twentieth Day of May One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six, in the Thirty-sixth Year of Our Reign.

GOD lave the King.

SEVERAL Members this Day appeared; and His Majesty having been pleased, by and with the Advice of His Privy Council, by an Order of Council, dated the 29th Day of July last, to declare, That the Parliament should be this Day again prorogued by Writ, the said Members went directly, without going into the House of Commons, or expecting any Mel-sage from the Lords, up to the Door of the House of Peers; and, after a short Stay there, the Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod opening the Door, they, with the Clerk, went up to the Bar of the House:, And they being the re, the Lord Chancellor standing up uncovered, declared that there was a Writ iilued under the Great Seal for further proroguing the Parliament unto Thursday the 15 th Day of next ensuing;

which Writ is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

fGEORGE the Third, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Irelan, King, Defender of the Faith, and so forth. To Our well-beloved and faithful the Prelates, Nobles, and Peers of Our Kingdom of Great Britain, and to Our beloved and faithful the

Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires and Burghs of Our said Kingdom, called and choion to Our Parliament, to be begun and held at Our City of Westminster, on the Sixteenth Day of August next, and to every of you, Greeting. Whereas We, for certain arduous and urgent Affairs, concerning Us, the State and Defence of Our Kingdom of Great Britain and the Church, did ordain the said Parliament to be begun and held at the City of Westminster, the Twelfth Day of July Instant; and did command you, by Our several Writs, to be present at the City and Day aforesaid, to treat, consent, and con-

clude, about those Things, which, in Our said Parliament, then and there should be proposed and treated of: And Whereas We have (by Our Writ) for certain Causes ar\d Considerations, Us thereunto especially moving, thought fit to prorogue Our said Parliament from the same Twelfth Day of July Instant, to and until the Sixteenth Day of August now next following; so that neither you, nor any of you, should be held or obliged to appear on the said Twelfth Day of July, at the aforesaid City, being willing that you, and every of you, be wholly discharged, as to Us, therefrom; and, by the same Writ, We very lately commanded you, and every of you, to appear, and be present, on the said Sixteenth Day of August, at Our said City, to treat, do, aft, and conclude, upon those Things, which, in Our said Parliament, should happen to be ordained: Nevertheless, for certain prelfing Causes and Considerations, Us especially thereunto moving, Our said Parliament, from the said Sixteenth Day of August, to and until Thursday the Fifteenth Day of September following, We have thought fit further to prorogue; so that neither you, nor any of you, should be held or obliged to appear on the said Sixteenth Day of , at the aforesaid City: We also will that you, and every of you, be wholly discharged, as to Us, therefrom; commanding, and, by the Tenor of these Presents, strictly requiring you, and every of you, and all others whom this may concern, That you, and every of you, do personally appear, and be present, on the said Fifteenth Day of September, at Our said City of , to

treat, do, aft, and conclude, upon those Things, which, in Our laid Parliament, by the Common Council of Our said Kingdom (by God's Abidance) shall happen to be ordained. Witness Ourself at , the

Twenty-ninth Day of July,in the Thirty-sixth Year of Our Reign.

By the KING Himself.

Signed with His own Hand.

A PROCLAMATION *

GEORGE R.

WHereas Our Parliament Hands prorogued to Thursday the Fifteenth Day of September next: We, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare Our Royal Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Fifteenth Day of September next, be held and fit for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs. And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and BurgelTes, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give their Attendance accordingly at West-mhifier, on the said Fifteenth Day of September next.

Given at Our Court at the Queen's House, the Twenty-ninth Day of July One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six, in the Thirty-sixth Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

And then the Lord Chancellor said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We have it in command from His Majesty to let you know. That His Majesty will, as soon as the Members of both Houses shall be sworn, in Person declare to you the Causes of His calling this Parliament; and it being necessary a Speaker of the House of Commons should be first chosen, it is His Majesty's Pleasure, that you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, do immediately repair to the Place where you are to fit; and there proceed to the Choice of some proper Person to be your Speaker; and that you present such Person, whom you shall so choose, here Tomorrow, at Twelve o'Clock, for His Majesty's Royal Approbation.

And the House being returned;

The Right honourable Lord Frederick Campbell, Commissioner for the Shire of Argyll, addressing himself to the Clerk (who Handing up, pointed to him, and then fat down) proposed to the House for their Speaker the Right honourable Henry Addington-, in which Motion he was seconded by Thomas Powys, Esquire, One of the Knights of the Shire for the County of Northampton-, and Major General Banajlre Tarletou, One of the Burgesses for the Borough of Liverpool, in the County of ter, also supported the said Motion.

The House then calling Mr. Addington to the Chair, he flood up in his Place, and expressed the Sense he had of the Honour proposed to be conferred upon him, and submitted himself to the House.

The House then again unanimously calling Mr. Addington to the Chair, he was taken out of his Place by the said Lord Frederick Campbell and Mr. Powys, and conducted by them to the Chair; where, Handing on the upper Step, he returned his humble Acknowledgments to the House for the great Honour they had been pleased to confer upon him, by unanimously choosing him to be again their Speaker.

And thereupon he fat down in the Chair; and then the Mace (which before lay under the Tabic) was laid upon the Table.

Then the Right honourable Henry Member

for the City of Edinburgh, and One of His Majesty's

principal Secretaries of State, having congratulated Mr. Speaker elect, moved that the House would adjourn till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

And the House accordingly adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock,

Mcrcuriiy 28° di Septembris;

Anno 36° Georgii III1" Regis, 1796.

THE House being met, and Mr. Speaker ele-ft having taken the Chair;

A Mellage was brought by Sir Francis Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers:

Accordingly Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went up to the House of Peers: Where Mr. Speaker cleft was presented to the said Lords Commissioners, for His Majesty's Royal Approbation: And

Then the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, One of the said Lords Commissioners, signified His Majesty's Approbation of Mr. Speaker cledt.

The House being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had been in the House of Peers: Where His Majesty was plcakd, by His Commissioners, to approve of the Choice ti.e House had made of him to be their Speaker; and that he had, in their Name, and on their Behalf, by humble Petition to His Majesty, laid Claim to all their ancient Rights and Privileges, particularly that their Perlqns, their Estates, and Sen-ants might be free from Arrests, and all Molestations; that they may enjoy Liberty of Speech in all their Debates; may have Accel's to His Majesty's Royal Person whenever Occasion shall require; and that all their Proceedings may receive from His Majesty the most favourable Construction; which, he said, His Majesty, by His said Commissioners, had confirmed to them in as full and ample Manner as they have been heretofore granted or allowed by His Majesty, or any of His Royal Predecessors.

And then Mr. Speaker repeated his most respectul Acknowledgments to the House, for the Honour they had done him.

Mr. Speaker then put the House in mind, that the first Thing to be done, was to take the Oaths, and make and subscribe the Declaration, and to take and subscribe the Oaths of Abjuration and Qualification, by Law required.

And thereupon Mr. Speaker, first alone, Handing upon the upper Step of the Clrair, took the said first -mentioned Oaths, and made and lubfcnlxd the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration, and also delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and took and subscribed the Oath of Qualification.

And, after him, several other Members took the said first-mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath' of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Resolved, That no Peer' of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to lerve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himtfelf to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the ufmost Severity against such Person.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is lit ting.

OrdbeJ, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Weshtiinster, do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Hall

shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made; by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster;and that he do fee the same put

in Execution.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Cafe, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person, to be appointed by the Post Master General, do for the future, every Day during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Riling of the House, and also from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters, and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered, and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Post Master General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame; and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

The apparently holtile Dispositions and Conduct of the Court of Madrid have led to Discussions of which I am not yet enabled to acquaint you with the final Result; but 1 am confident that, whatever may be their Ilfue, I shall have given to Europe a further Proof of My Moderation and Forbearance; and I can have no Doubt of your Determination to defend, against every Aggrefiion, the Dignity, Rights, and Interests, of the British Empire.

Mr. Speaker Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had this Day Kmp'sthe attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where

Sp«tcli. His Majesty was pleased to make a moil Gracious

Speech from the Throne to both Hov.fes of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mif-takes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is a peculiar Satisfaction to Me, in the present Conjuncture of Affairs, to recur to your Advice, after the recent Opportunity which has been given for collecting the Sense of My People, engaged in a difficult and arduous Contest, for the Preservation of all that is most dear to Us.

I have omitted no Endeavours far setting on Toot Negotiations to restore Peace to , and to secure

for the future the general Tranquillity. — The Steps which I have taken for this Purpose, have at length opened the Way to an immediate and direct Negotiation, the Ilfue of which mull either produce the desirable End of a just, honourable, and l'olid Peace, for Us, and for Our Allies, or must prove, beyond Dispute, to what Caule alone the Prolongation of the Calamities of War must be aferibed.

I shall immediately fend a Person to Paris, with full Powers to treat for this Object; and it is My anxious Wilh that this Measure may lead to the Restoration of general Peace: But you mull be sensible that nothing can so much contribute to give Effect to this Desire, as your manifesting that we possess both the Determination and the Resources to oppose, with increased Activity and Energy, the further Efforts with which we may have to contend.

You will feel this peculiarly necessary at a Moment when the Enemy has openly manifested the Intention of attempting a Descent on these Kingdoms. — It cannot be doubted, what would be the Ilfue of such an Enterprize; but it befits your Wisdom to neglect no Precautions that may either preclude the Attempt, or secure the Ipeedieft Means of turning it to the Confusion and Ruin of the Enemy.

In reviewing the Events of the Year, you will have observed that, by the Skill and Exertions of My Navy, Our extensive and increasing Commerce has been protected to a Degree almoll beyond Example; and the Fleets of the Enemy have, for the greatclt Part of the Year, been blocked up in their own Ports.

The Operations in the East and Indies have been highly honourable to the British Arms, and productive of great National Advantage; and the Valour and good Conduct of My Forces, both by Sea and Land, have been eminently conspicuous.

The Fortune of War on the Continent has been more various, and the Progress of the French Armies threatened, at one Period, the utmost Danger to all

Europe; but, from the honourable and dignified Perseverance of My Ally the Emperor, and from the Intrepidity, Discipline, and invincible Spirit, of the Austrian Vol. 52.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I rely on your Zeal and Public Spirit for such Supplies as you may think necessary for the Service of the Year. It is a great Satisfaction to Me to observe that, notwithstanding the temporary Embarrassments which have been experienced, the State of the Commerce, Manufactures, and Revenue, of the Country, proves the reaf Extent and Solidity of Our Resources, and furnilhes you such Means as must be equal to any Exertions which the present Crisis may require.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Distrefies which tvere in the last Year experienced from the Scarcity of Corn, are now, by the Blessing of God, happily removed; and an abundant Harvest affords the pleasing Prospect of Relief in that important Article to the labouring Classes of the Community. — Our internal Tranquillity has also continued undisturbed-The general Attachment of My People to the British Constitution has appeared on every Occasion; and the Endeavours of those, who wished to introduce Anarchy and Confusion into this Country, have been repreifed by the Energy and Wisdom of the Laws. .

To defeat all the Designs of Our Enemies, to restore to My People the Blefiings of a secure and honourable Peace, to maintain inviolate their Religion, Laws, and Liberty, and to deliver down unimpaired to the latest Posterity the Glory and Happiness of these Kingdoms, is the constant Wilh of My Heart, and the uniform End of all My Actions. — In every Measure that can conduce to these Objects, I am confident of receiving the firm, zealous, and affectionate Support of My Parliament.

Carmarthen A Petition of John George Philipps, Esquire, was dtion otTlr?- read; Setting forth. That on Friday, the 27th Day of Philipps. May last, an Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the County of the Borough of Carmarthen camp on, in the Guildhall there, and was continued and ended on Saturday the 28th Day of the same Month, at which Election the Petitioner and Magens Dorrien Magens, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the Petitioner was duly elected by a great Majority of legal Votes, but that Evan Evans and David Lewis, Gentlemen, who were the Sheriffs of the said Borough and who acted as Returning Officers at the said Elec tion, in taking the Poll were guilty of the greatest Partiality and Injustice towards the Petitioner, by illegally rejecting the Votes of several Burgesses who had a legal Right to vote, and who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, and by admitting other Persons to vote for the said Magens Dorrien Magens, who had no legal Right to vote; and that the said Sheriffs, although they had, at the Opening the Poll, declared that the Statute passed in the Third Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to " prevent occasional Freemen from voting at Elections " of Members to serve in Parliament for Cities and " Boroughs/' did not apply to the Bojough of Carmarthen, and fiad, in Consequence of such Declaration, permitted Four Burgesses, who had not been possessed of their Franchises Twelve Calendar Months, to poll for the said Magens Dorrien Magens, yet the said Sheriffs immediately afterwards rejected Seventeen Burgesses, who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, merely because they had not been possessed of their Franchises Twelve Calendar Months next pre- ceding the Election; and the said Sheriffs were guilty of several other gross Acts of Misconduct and Partiality in Favour of the said Magens Dorrien Magens, and a gain ft the Petitioner; and that, by thcle and oti er undue Means and Proceedings, a pretended Majority hath been procured in Favour of the said Magens Dor-ricti Magens, who hath been thereupon returned, by the said Sheriffs, as the Member to serve in Parliament for the County of the Borough of Carmarthen, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had an undoubted Majority of legal Votes tendered at such Election, and was duly elected, and ought to have been returned, and also to the great Prejudice of the legal Electors of the said County Borough, and in Defiance of the Freedom of Election: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant to the Petitioner such Relief therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday, the 27th Day of this Instant October, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon'.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records,

" Obligation, or Engagement to do the laine, either " to any such Person or Persons in particular, or to " any such County, City, Town, Port, or Borough,

" in general, or to or fur the Use or Benefit of them " or any of them, every such Entertainment, Prelent,

" Gift, Reward, Promise, Obligation, or Engagement,

" is by this House declared to be Bribery, and such " Entertainment, Present, Gift, Reward, Promise,

" Obligation, or Engagement, being duly proved, is " and shall be sufficient Ground, Cause, and Matter,

" to make every such Election void as to the Person " so offending, and to render the Person so elected incapable to fit in Parliament by such Election;" and that by an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for preventing Charge and Expence in Elections " of Members to serve in Parliament," reciting, that,

" Whereas grievous Complaints are made, and manifestly appear to be true, in the Kingdom, of undue " Elections of Members to Parliament, by excessive " and exorbitant Expences, contrary to the Laws, and " in Violation of the Freedom due to the Election of " Representatives for the Commons of England in " Parliament, to the great Scandal of the Kingdom,

" dishonourable, and may be destructive to the Constitution of Parliaments, wherefore, for Remedy " therein, and that all Elections of Members to Parliament may be hereafter freely and indifferently " made without Charge or Expence," it was Enacted and Declared, that no Person or Persons thereafter to be elected to serve in Parliament for any County, City,

Town, Borough, Port, or Place, within the Kingdom of England, after the Teste of the Writ of Summons to Parliament, or after the Teste, or the issuing out, or ordering of the Writ or Writs of Election, upon the calling or summoning of any Parliament thereafter, or after any such Place should become vacant thereafter, in the Time of the then present, or of any other Parliament, should thereafter, by himself or them selves, or by any other Ways or Means on his or their Behalf, or at his or their Charge, before his or their Election to serve in Parliament for any County, j

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subicfls,

ought to have been returned as duly defied with the the Commons of in Parliament alFm-

Vol. 52. bled,

16 7° — 8° OBobris. . 1796".

bled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty our humble and unanimous Thanks for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We are truly sensible of Your Majesty's parental Regard for the Interest of Your Subjects, in having omitted no Endeavours for letting on Foot Negotiations to restore Peace to Eur, and to secure for the future the general Tranquillity; and we rejoice to learn, that the Steps which have been taken for this Purpose, have at length opened the Way to an immediate and direct Negotiation, which, we doubt net, will be lb conducted on Your Majesty's Part, as either to produce the desirable End of a just, honourable, and l'olid Peace, for us and for our Allies, or to prove beyond Dispute to what Cause alone the Prolongation of the Calamities of War must be aicribed.

We cordially join with Your Majesty in an anxious With that the Step, which Your Majesty proposes to take, of fending a Person to Paris with full Powers to treat, may lead to the Restoration of general Peace; but we are fully sensible that nothing can lb much contribute to give Eiled to this Desire, as manifesting that we pollels both the Determination and the Resources to oppose, with increased Activity and Energy, the further Efforts with which we may have to contend; and we must indeed feel this to be peculiarly necessary when an Intention has been openly manifested of attempting a Descent on thel'e Kingdoms; and, although it cannot be doubted w'hat would be the Issue of such an Enterprize, we deem it an indispensable Duty to neglect no Precautions that may either preclude the Attempt, or secure the speediest Means of turning it to the Confusion and Ruin of the Enemy.

In reviewing the Events of the Year, we have not failed to observe with a just Satisfaction, that, by the Skill and Exertions of Your Majesty's Navy, our extensive and increasing Commerce has been protected to a Degree almost beyond Example; and that the Fleets of the Enemy have, for the greatest Part of the Year, been blocked up in their own Ports; and we have fecn with Pleasure the Operations in the East and West Indies, which, while they have been productive

of great National Advantage, have also dilplayed the Valour and good Conduct of Your Majesty's Forces, both by Sea and Land, in a Degree highly honourable to the British Arms.

Having contemplated with anxious Solicitude the various Fortune of War on the Continent, and the Danger with which all Europe was at one Time threatened, we relied with proportionable Admiration and Joy on the honourable and dignified Perseverance of Your Majesty's Ally the Emperor, and on the Intrepidity, Discipline, and invincible Spirit, of the AuJIrian Forces under the auspicious Conduct of the Archduke Charles-, and we entertain the most: /anguine Hope that, from the Turn lately given to the Course of the War, the find Result of the Campaign may prove more disastrous to the Enemy than its Commencement and Progress, for a Time, were favourable to their

the most cordial Satisfaction to find that, notwithstanding the temporary EmbarralfinCnts which have been experienced, the State of the Commerce, Manufactures, and Revenue of the Country, proves the real t Extent and Solidity of the Public Resources, and will furnish such Means as may be equal to the great and vigorous Exertions which the present Crilis peculiarly requires.

We acknowdedge with the utmost Thankfulnels and Satisfaction, that the Distrefi'es, which were in the lait Year experienced from the Scarcity of Corn, are now, by the Blelfing of God, happily removed, and that an abundant Harvest affords the pleasing Prolped of Relief on that important Article to the labouring ClallLs of the Community; and with equal Satisfaction we refled on the uninterrupted Continuance cf our internal Tranquillity, on the general Attachment of Your Majesty's faithful Subjects to the British Constitution, and on the happy Effects produced by the Energy and Wisdom of the Laws in reprefiing the Endeavours of those who wifiicd to introduce Anarchy and Confulion into the Country.

We beseech Your Majesty to believe that we arc deeply imprested with the gracious and paternal Expressions of Your Majesty's conliant Solicitude for the Glory and Happinels of Your Kingdoms; and w'c are persuaded that Your Majesty may at all Times rely on the firm, zealous, and afiedionafe, Support of Your Parliament in those Exertions which are directed to the great Objcd of defeating all the Dd'gns of our Enemies, of restoring to the People the s of a

secure and honourable Peace, and of delivering down unimpaired, to the latest Posterity, those Civil and Religious BIcflings by which theft Kingdoms have been so eminently distinguished under the 1'rotedion of Your Majesty's just and auspicious Government.

and that the Petitioner, nevertheless, conceives, and is advised, that he was duly elected, and ought to have been returned as the Commissioner, or Member, for the said Class or District of Boroughs, because the Elections of the said John Gi/christ, Patrick Geddes, and David Williamson, as Commissioners, or Delegates, for the respective Boroughs aforesaid, were all, and each of them, brought about by undue Means, made by unqualified Persons, were illegal, and contrary to the Statutes made and provided for regulating the Elections of Commissioners, or Delegates, to chuse Burgesses to represent the Boroughs of in the Parliament of Great Britain, and likewise contrary to the Statutes regulating the Choice of such Burgesses, and Otherwise informal and void, and because the Commissions, pretended to be given to the said Persons severally, were also illegal, informal, and essentially defective, and that the Majority of legal Votes at the said Election were in Favour of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take his Petition into their Consideration, to allow him to be heard by his Coun-fel thereon, and to grant to him such Relief in the Prc-mises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Memorandum:

By the Act passed in 1781, intituled, ct An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of " Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies, &c." the East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in Proportion to the Number of Troops few, or to be sent to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum 'the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only; and as it will be necessary to provide for the Subsistence of the Four Recruiting Troops, and Nine Recruiting Companies, remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present for this Purpose, the Sum o(£. 13,335. 18r. which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the above Estimate.

" between His Majesty and the United States of " rica, signed at London the 19th of November 1794."

And the Title of the said Paper was read.

The said Paper is as follovyeth; viz.

EXPLANATORY ARTICLE, signed at Philadelphia, the 4th of A lay 1796, to be added to the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, between His Majesty and the United States of Ame» rica, signed at London, the 19th of November 1794.

Whereas by the Third Article of the Treaty of Amity,

Commerce, and Navigation, concluded at London, on the 19th Day of November 1794, between His Britannich Majesty and the United States of A, it was agreed. That it should atallTimes be free to His Majesty's Sub-

M jects,

42 18° OBobris. . 1796.

jests, and to the Citizens of the United States, and also to the Indians dwelling on either Side of the Boundary Line assigned by the Treaty of Peace to the United States, freely to pass and repass, by Land or Inland Navigation, into the respective Territories and Countries of the Two Con trading Parties, on the Continent of America, (the Country within the Limits of the Bay

Company only excepted) and to navigate all the Lakes, Rivers, and Waters thereof, and freely to carry on Trade and Commerce with each other, l'ubjeft to the Provisions and Limitations contained in the said Article: And whereas, by the Eighth Article of the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, concluded at , on the

3d Day of August 1795, between the United States and the Nations or Tribes of Indians called The Wyandots, Delawares, Shawanoes, Ottowas , Putawati-

rnies, Mi amis. Eel River, Weeas, Kickapoos, and Kajkajkias, it was stipulated, that no Person should be permitted to reside at any of the Towns or Hunting Camps of the said Indian Tribes as a Trader, who is not furnished with a Licence for that Purpose under the Authority of the United States; which latter Stipulation has excited Doubts whether in its Operation it may not interfere with the due Execution of the said Third Article of the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation; and it being the sincere Delire of His Majesty, and of the United States, that this Point should be so explained as to remove all Doubts, and promote mutual Satisfaction and Fricndship; and for this Purpose His Britamick Majesty, having named for his Commis-

fioner PhineasBend, El'quire, His Majesty's Consul Gene-

ral for the Middle and Southern States of America, (and now His Majesty's Charge d'Affaires to the United States) and the President of the United States having named for their Commissioner Timothy Pickering, Esquire, Secretary of State of the United States, to whom, agreeably to the Laws of the United States, he has entrusted this Negotiation; they, the said Commissioners, having communicated to each other their Full Powers, have, in virtue of the fame, and conformably to the Spirit of the last Article of the said Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, entered into this Explanatory Article, and do by these Presents explicitly agree and declare, that no Stipulations in any Treaty, subsequently concluded by either of the Contracting Parties with any other State or Nation, or with any Indian Tribe, can be understood to derogate in any Manner from the Rights of free Jntfcr-course and Commerce, secured by the aforesaid Third Article of the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, to the Subjects of His Majesty, and to the Citizens of the United States, and to the Indians dwelling on either Side of the Boundary Line aforesaid; but that all the said Persons shall remain at full Liberty freely to pals and repass, by Land or Inland Navigation, into the respective Territories and Countries of the Contracting Parties on either Side of the said Boundary Line, and freely to carry on Trade and Commerce with each other, according to the Stipulations of the said Third Article -of the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation.

This Explanatory Article, when the same shall have been ratified by His Majesty, and by the President of the United States by and with the Advice and Consent of their Senate, and the respective Ratifications mutually exchanged, shall be added to, and make a Part of the said Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, and shall be permanently binding upon His Majesty and the United States.

In Witness whereof, We, the said Commissioners of His Majesty the King of Great Britain and the United States of America, have signed this present Explanatory Article, and thereto affixed Our Seals.

Done at Philadelphia,this Fourth Day of May, in the Year of our Lord One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six.

P. Bond. (L. S.) Timothy Pickering. (L. S.)

Anno 36® Georgii III"1 Regis, 1796. Prayers.

SEVERAL Petitions, complaining of undue Elections and Returns, being offered to be presented to the House, the same were delivered in at the Table; and One of the said Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of being in the Third Class mentioned in the Resolution of the House of the 7th Day of this Instant October (One of the Sitting Members for the said Borough being returned to serve for Two Places) the said Petition was read; as followeth; viz.

A Petition of certain Electors of the Borough of Tregony, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was read; Setting forth, That, at the last Election for Burgestes to serve in Parliament for the Borough of in the County of CornwallSir Lionel , Baronet, and John Nicholls, Esquire, Sir John Baronet, and

Philip Metcalfe, Esquire, were Candidates; and that at

the said Election many indirect and unwarrantable Practices were made Use of by the said Sir Copley and John Nicholls, and other Persons in their Interest, to procure a colourable Majority for them; and that Richard Gurney, Clerk, the Returning Officer, did, before the Poll, attempt by improper influence, to prevail upon Persons, who had no Right to vote, to appear, and tender their Votes in Favour of the said Sir Lionel Copley and John Nicholls, promising, and giving them Rca-lons to believe, that he would admit them upon the Poll, and that during the Poll, he behaved with marked Partiality towards the said Sir Lionel Copley and Nicholls, and did illegally admit a great Number of Voters, who had no Right to poll at the said Election, to vote for the said Sir Lionel Copley and John Nicholls, and did wilfully reject many others who tendered their Votes for the said Sir John Doyley and Philip;

and that the said Richard Gurney was, previous to and during the Poll, guilty of gross Bribery, as well by giving as by promising to give Money and other Rewards to the said Voters, and did thereby, and by other corrupt Means, prevail on many of the Voters to vote for the said Sir Lionel Copley and Jo Nicholls, and that, previous to and during the Poll, the said Sir Copley

and John Nicholls, were by themselves, and by their Agents, guilty of many Acts of Bribery, and allowed to the Electors of the said Borough Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, and Provision, by which Means, by Threats, by Promises, and by other corrupt Practices and Proceedings, the said Sir Lionel Copley and John Nicholls have procured themselves to be unduly returned to serve in the present Parliament for the said Borough, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners, and in Violation of the Rights and Privileges of the said Borough, and of the Commons of England: And therefore, on Behalf of themselves and other Electors of the said Borough, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant to them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday, the 10th Day of November next, at a Quarter of an Hour after Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

and that the said Sir William Geary was, by himtelf or his Agents, guilty, of Bribery and Corruption, and pther corrupt, illegal, and unwarrantable Practices, in order to procure Persons to vote for 1 iin at the said Election; and that he the said Sir William Geary did, by himself, his Friends, or Agents, before or during the said Election, enter into an illegal and corrupt Bargain or Agreement with the said Sir Edward , his

Friends, or Agents, relative to the Expence to be borne by the said Sir William Geary at the said Election, the said Sir William Geary, by himself, his Friends, or Agents, undertaking and promiiing to the said Sir Edward Knatchbul I, his Friends, or Agents, to bear a much greater Proportion of the Expence of the said Election than would otherwise have fallen to his Share, whereby the said Sir Edward his Friends,

or Agents, agreed, and became bound, to procure Persons to poll for the said Sir William Geary, at the said Election, who would not otherwise have given their Votes in his Favour; and that the said Sir William Geary did, by himself, his Friends, or Agents, enter into some other corrupt Agreement or Agreements relative to the Expence of the said Election, contrary to Law, and in Violation of the Freedom of Election, and of the Rights of the Petitioners: That the Petitioners are advil'ed, and believe, that the apparent Majority in Favour of Sir William Geary over Mr. Hollywood arose from John Mumford, Esquire, the High Sheriff of the said County, having taken upon Jiimfelf arbitrarily, illegally, unjustly, and partially, to admit many Persons to poll for the said Sir William Geary, who ought to have b"en rejected, and having arbitrarily, illegally, unjand partially, rejected the Votes of many Freeholders who tendered their Votes for the said Filmer Honyzvood-, that the Petitioners do therefore assert, and are ready to prove, that the Majority of legal Votes at the said Election was in Favour of the said Filmer Honyzvood, Esquire; that the said Sir William Geary ought not to have been returned, but that the said Filmer Honyzvood ought to have been returned one of the Knights of the Shire to represent the said County of Kent in this present Parliament; and that the Petitioners, being by the Means hereinbefore set forth; viz. by the illegal and partial Conduct of the High Sheriff, and by the corrupt and unlawful Acts, Bargains, and Agreements, of the said Sir Edward Knatchbul! and Sir William Geary, and others, their Friends and Agents, deprived of being represented in Parliament by their true and legal Representative Filmer Honyzvood, pray the House to take their same into Consideration, to order the Name of the said Sir William Geary to be erased from the Return, and that of the said Filmer Honszvood, Esquire, to be inserted in dead thereof, or to order the Return of the said Sir William Geary to be declared void, or to administer to them such other Relief in the Premises as to the Wisdom of the House shall seem meet.

That, by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for augmenting the " Number of Canons Residentiary in the Cathedral " Church of Litchfield, and for improving the Deaniy " and Prebends in the said Cathedral Church," it was (amongst other Things) made lawful to and for the Bishop of Litchfield and Coventry, for the Time being, to confer Two or Three Prebends of the Cathedral Church of Litchfield on one and the same Person, provided that the Person, collated to such Second or Third Prebend, should be obliged to perform such Ref.dence as the local Statutes of the said Cathedral Church lliould require, he hating a Prebendal House in the Close, wherein to relidc, and that the Prebends, lo united, should for ever continue together, and, with the House, be from Time to Time conferred upon one and the same Person; and that successive Bishops of Litchfield and Coventry, in pursuance of the Powers given by the said Act, have confuted Two Prebends upon each of Four of the Prebendaries of the said Church, who have been since called Canons Residentiary of the new Foundation; but, inasmuch as the said Act did not direct, that the Prebendaries, who might have Two Prebends conferred upon them by virtue of the said Act, should have a Vote in the Chapter of the said Cathedral Church, consisting of the Dean and Four Canons Residentiary of the old Foundation, nor any Participation of the common Revenues of the said . Chapter, they have never been admitted Members of the Chapter of Dean and Canons Residentiary, or to a Participation of the common Revenues of the said Chapter, and the Dean and Four Canons Residentiary of the old Foundation, or the Majority of them, have continued to do all Acts of the Chapter of Dean and, Canons Residentiary, exclusively of the Prebendaries now called Canons Residentiary of the new Foundation; and the Petitioners conceive it expedient, that all who are Canons Residentiary of the said Cathedral Church should be Members of the said Chapter of Dean and Canons Residentiary, and have an equal Interest in all the Concerns of the said Cathedral Church, but the common Revenues of the said Chapter of Dean and Canons Residentiary are too small and insufficient even for the Maintenance of Four Canons Residentiary; and that an equal Participation among the Canons Residentiary of the said Cathedral Church, of the common Revenues of the said Chapter of Dean and Canons Residentiary, might conveniently take place, if the whole Number of Canons Residentiary were fixed to be Six (which was the Number of Canons Kefiden-tiary anciently) and an Addition were made to the Income of the Canons Residentiary of the old Foundation; and that Doubts may arile, whether Elections and other Acts, done by the Dean and Chapter, consisting of the Dean and Four Canons Residentiary of the old Foundation, are the Acts of the Dean and Chapter of the said Cathedral Church, and the Petitioners conceive the same should be declared valid, and that all Acts which shall be hereafter done by the Dean and Chapter aforesaid, until the Regulations before-mentioned take Efieft, should be deemed good and valid in Law; and that the Fund, called The Fabric Fund, which is appropriated to keeping in Repair the Cathedral Church of L aforesaid, has been found

very insufficient, and several large Sums of Money have been lately expended in the Repairs of the said Cathedral Church, and considerable Sums are now due and owing on the Credit of the said Fund, the common and ordinary Revenues whereof are very inadequate to the Discharge of the Sums so due, and to the necessary 8

Repairs of the said Church; and that tire Petitioners conceive it is expedient and proper that the said Fabric Fund should be improved and augmented; and that there is no Building specially appropriated for the Registry of the Dioceie of Litchfield and , and for

depositing the Wilis and Muniments within and belonging to the said Dioceie, and the Petitioners conceive it is of great Importance that there should be a lafe and sufficient Building appropriated for those Pur-' poses: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to explain and amend the said Act of the Fourth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, to repeal Part thereof, and for other the Purposes before-mentioned, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Edward Littleton, the Karl Gozver Sutherland, &c.: And they are to meet To- morrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to lend lor Persons, Papers, and Records.

of the Peace, held at the Castle of for the said

County, on the 5th Day of 1796, waspresented

to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the County of Norfolk is a large and populous County, and the Common Gaol, or Prison, thereof, is at the Castle of Norwich, which is nearly in the Centre of the said County; and that the Summer Assizes, as well as the General Quarter Session of the Peace, have been constantly held at the Castle of Norwich, and the Lent Assizes have usually been held at the Borough of ford; and that the said Borough of is Thirty

Miles distant from the Castle of Norwich, from whence the Prisoners are obliged to be conveyed to fhetford previous to their Trials, and back again after Conviction, to the great Charge of the County, it being necessary to hire a G uard to prevent Escapes; and that the said Borough of Thetford, being situated at the Extremity of the said County, the greater Part of the Prosecutors, Witnesses, and Suitors, are obliged to travel upwards of Fifty Miles from their several Places of Abode, to attend the Assizes there, to the great Inconvenience of Individuals, and at a considerable additional Expence to the County at large: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the holding the Lent Assizes for the County of Norfolk at the said Castle of Norwich.

That, by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, several Roads leading from the at /

" Street ,to Beckbury and the New Inn, and from the " Birches Brook to the Hand Post, in the Parish of " Kemberton,in the County of Salop," several Tolls

were granted, and Powers given for widening and keeping in Repair the several Roads, and for putting the said Act in Execution; and, by another Act, passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for continuing the Term and Powers of the last-men-2

tioned Act, and for making the same more effectual, the said former Act was continued from the Expiration thereof for the further Term of Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and that the Trustees, appointed by the said recited Acts, have made great Progress in the Execution thereof, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money, which, together with the Tolls, have been faithfully applied; but the said Roads cannot be well and sufficiently widened, amended, and kept in Repair, nor the Money already borrowed be repaid, unless the Term and Powers granted by the said Acts be continued, altered, enlarged amended, and rendered more effectual; and that, if the said Turnpike Roads were extended, by making a new Branch of Road in Addition to, and to communicate with, the said Roads and to lead out of the same at the Bottom of Lincoln Hill, in the Parish of Made/ey, in the said County of , and from thence through the several Parillies of Made-ley, Sutton, Maddock, and Stockton, in the said County, to join the present Turnpike Road, at or near the End of a Lane leading out of the said Roads to the Village of Norton, in the said Parish of Stockton; and if the said new Branch of Road, and the said present Turnpike Roads were fomade to communicate, and were united, and put under the Care and Management of the same Trustees, and if the Tolls to be taken on all the said Roads were made one consolidated Fund for Payment of the Monies borrowed, and which may be borrowed, on the Credit thereof, wdth Interest for the fame, it would not only tend to the Advancement of the'foils, and the Benefit of all the said Roads, but would the looner enable the Trustees to make the said intended new Branch of Road, and to widen, amend, and keep the lame, and the said other Turnpike Roads, in Repair; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, if the said new Branch of Road was so made, the same would be of great Pub lie Utility, by opening a much nearer and more easy Communication between SCoalbrook Dale, Made/ey, Brofe/ey, Bent ha//, Dudley, and Birmingham:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for farther continuing the Term granted by the said Act of the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty; and for amending, altering, enlarging, and making more effectual, the Powers and Authorities granted by the said Two several Acts hereinbefore stated; and also for extending the said prcilnt Turnpike Roads, by making a new Branch of Road, to communicate with the said present Turnpike Road at the Bottom of Lincoln Hill, in the said Parish of Madcley, and to lead from thence through the said several Parishes of Made/ey, Sutton, Maddock, and Stockton, in the said County of Salop, into, and to communicate with, the said original Turnpike Road, at or near the End of the said Lane leading out of the same Turnpike to the Village of Norton, in the Pari fit o aforesaid, and

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized, by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of , and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Earl of Liverpool, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth;

Sendee of His Majesty's Army and Navy:

Day appointed forconlidering the Report on Trent and Mersey Canal Bill

A Message from the Lords by Mr. Leeds and Mr. Smith:

Mr. Speaker, .

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, A‘n Act to indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments, and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications, within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been loll or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the Execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors; and for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants and Officers of the Militia, who have ne-gledled to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace within the Time limited by Law, and for allowing further Time for that Purpose; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew;

Ordered, That the Report which was made from the Committee, to whom the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey, to make a Navigable Canal from, and out of, a certain Branch of their said Navigation, called The Cal-don Canal, within the Liberty of Endon, to the Town of Leek, in the County of Stafford, and also a Refer-voir for supplying the said Canals with Water, was committed, be taken into further Consideration upon tiefday Sevennight, the 7th Day of December next.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Robert Biddulph, Esquire; and also, the Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, being lawful Electors of the Borough of Leo-minster, in the County of Ifereford, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions. ....

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

<\nd he went accordingly.

And being returned; >

And several Members returned upon new Writs, and several Members present, having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, and several of them having delivered in an Account of their Qualifications, and taken arid subscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hun-dted and Ninety Members being present;

The Counfei and Agents were called in to the Bar. And the Door of the House being locked; .

The Orders of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration, were read.

And the Names of Forty-one Members, then present; were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Names of Eight other Members, then present, were drawn, who were, not objected to.

Eyemouth A Petition of the Freeholders, Heritors, and Farmers, titfcm°Ur PC" the County of Berwick, and of the Merchants, Ship-malters, and other Inhabitants, of the Town o( Eyemouth, thereunto subscribing, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Port of Eyemouth is the only Harbour within the County of

wick, from which great Part of the Corn, and other Productions of the County, have been exported; and a considerable Trade is carried on there from the Baltic and Norway, and in the Importation of Coal, Lime, and other Commodities, and it is of singular Advantage to the Coalting Trade, being of ealy Access in all Weathers, particularly in Storms from the North, and North East, and, lying in the Corner of an extensive Bay, Ships, coming in for Shelter, can work out at all Times, and in all Winds, 'when it is safe to go to Sea, so that they can never remain Wind-bound; and that, moved by thele Considerations of its Importance and Utility, the Landholders of this County, and their Tenants, and the Merchants in Eyemouth, and others interested, have, at different Times, expended considerable Sums of Money, which they raised by Subscriptions, for building a Pier and other Bulwarks necessary for the Safety and Security of the Shipping: That a Pier was built in 1752, which coll about £. 1,500, and a Breakwater in 1772, under the Direction of the late Mr. Smeaton, which coll about £. 2,500, and which answered all the good Effects ex-peCled from them; but, as no Fund was provided for keeping them in Repair, and being expoftd to successive Injuries, from Land Floods and Sea Storms, they ar now in many Parts much decayed and weakened, and by an extraordinary Land Flood, in November 1794, a great Part of the Foundation of the old Pier was undermined, and much damaged, and has lince tumbled into the River, by which the Harbour is not only rendered incommodious, but difficult of Access, and unsafe for the Shipping frequenting it; and that the Convention of the Royal Burghs of Scotland, fenlible of the Diiad-yantage and Danger to the Vessels employed in- the Coalting Trade, from the ruinous State of this Harbour, did, at their annual Meeting, in lall, allow to assist in repairing it, and the Landholders of this County, and others, have, in Addition to that £.300, already lubscribed the Sum of800, which, from Elti-mates ready to be produced, and further Subscriptions expected it appears will be sufficient to repair the Pier and Breakwater, and also to make the other necessary Improvements, for enlarging, scouring, and deepening the Harbour, and for rendering it safe and commodious in Time coming; but the Expences, to be laid out in the Execution of thele Works, will also be loll to the Subscribers, and to the Public, unless a Fund be provided for supporting the Pier and Breakwater, and the Other proposed Improvements; and that the Petitioners are advised, the proper Fund for this Purpose will be Certain small Duties on the Trade and Shipping frequenting this Port, which cannot be levied without the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to give Leave for bringing in a Bill, to authorize the levying of certain small Duties on the Trade and Shipping in the Port of Eyemouth, in the County of Berwick, to be applied for the Purposes aforesaid, under Inch Regulations as the House in its Wildom shall think jult and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do exa-Vol. 52.

Then the said Petition was delivered in, and read; Setting forth, That at the last Election for a Member to serve in Parliament for the County of Flinty held on the 8th Day of November 1 796, Sir Thomas Mojlyn, Baronet, and the Petitioner, together with the Honourable Lloyd Kenyon, were the only Candidates, and that a Majority of Votes were given for Sir Thomas Mcflyn; that the Petitioner had the greateli Number of Votes next to Sir Thomas Mojlyn, and the Honourable Lloyd Kenyon had the smallest Number of Votes upon the Poll; and the Petitioner has been advised and informed, and is ready to prove, that he is entitled to repreicnr the said County in Parliament, as having the greatest Number of Votes of those Candidates who are legally qualified to fit in Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take his same into Conficleration, and to permit him to be heard, by his Counsel, thereon, and to grant to him such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of James John Vajfar, Esquire, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner was a Candidate at the last Election for 6

the Bdrough of Malmfibury, together with Philip Met-

calfs, Esquire: That the Borough of Malmfibury is an ancient Borough, and from Time immemorial, or from a very early Period, hath font Members to Parliament; and that the Men and Free Burgefl'es of the said Borough have, from Time immemorial, or by divers ancient Charters, been incorporated by the Name of The Alderman and Burgesses of the Borough of Malmfibury; and that the Right of Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, is in all the Members of the said Corporate Body, or in the Burgesses of the said Borough, and not in the Capital Burgesses of the said Borough only, nor in any select Body of the said Corporation; and that a large Majority of the said Burgefl'es tendered their Votes to the Returning Officer of the said Borough, in Favour of the Petitioner, and that the said Returning Officer admitted on the Poll, for the Sitting Member, several Votes which were illegal, or otherwise objeftionable, and rcjefted many Votes that ought to have been admitted on the Poll for the Petitioner; and that the said Returning Officer acted partially and unjuflifiably, and under the Operation of a corrupt and illegal System of Influence, and Practices, which has, for Years past, notoriously violated, and continues to violate, the Freedom of Election in the said Borough, and hath been destructive of the fair, legal, and constitutional Mode of electing Members to serve in Parliament; and that the Petitioner conceives the Sitting Member was unduly returned for the said Borough, and that the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to have been returned:

And therefore praying, That the House will order the Return for the said Borough to be amended, and the Name of the Petitioner to be inserted in the Place of the Sitting Member, or to grant to the Petitioner such other Redress as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday, the 7th Day of March next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of several Acts, made for regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necefihry by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of the several. Persons, whose Names alt; thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Traders, and Inhabitants of the County of Northumberland and Town and County of Newcastle-upen-Tyne, was presented to

the House, and read; Setting forth. That there is a considerable Intercourse in Point of Trade, carried on by Land Carriage, between the Town of Neivcastle-upon-Tjne and the City of Car/iJJe, and other Parti of the County of Cumberland, and also between the said Town of Newcastle-upon-Tyne and the Welhern Parts of the County of Northumberland-, that the Country, through which the Roads between the said Places lie, is very hilly, and the Passage attended with Difficulty; ttnd that, by proper Surveys and Levels lately made and taken, it appears that a Navigable Cut or Canal may be made, from the said Town of Tyne,to a Place called Hay don Bridge, in the said County of Northumberland, there to communicate with a Turnpike Road, leading through the Town of Halt-whijile, in the said County of Northumberland, to the City of Carlisle aforesaid; that, by such Navigable Cut or Canal, a considerable Length of Land Carriage would be saved, and the Conveyance of Lead, Coals, Lime, Limestone, and other Mines, Minerals, and Merchandize, be much facilitated; and that it would tend to the Improvement of the adjacent Lands, and moreover be of great Public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining such Navigable Cut or Canal, in such Manner, with such Powers and Provisions, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Grey, Mr. &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

MR. John Pitt reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for naturalizing Adriaen

de Gruyter Vink, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment: And he delivered the Bill in at the Clerk's Table.

Ordered, That the Bill be ingrafted.

Mr: Dickinson, Senior, reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open and Commonable Failures within the Parish of West oh Zoyland, in the County of Somerset, was committed; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Owners of Six Common Rights and an Half, who are neuter; and also the Owners of One Fourth of a Freehold Right, and the Owners of Two Fifths of Two Leasehold Rights; who could not be met with; and that the whole Number of Common Rights is One hundred and Twenty-eight; and that no Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill); and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to

report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

A Petition of the several Persons, whole Names are Chatham thereunto subscribed, Trustees, amongst others, ap- dsPeti' pointed for putting in Execution the several Acts herein after mentioned, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That, by Two several Acts, passed in the Third and Seventeenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing and widening the Road from that Part of Chatham which lies next to the City of Rochester,to Saint Crop, near the City of Canterbury, in the County of Kent, and for repealing so much of a former Ad as appropriates Part of the Money, arising by the Tolls or Duties therein mentioned, towards repairing the Road between the Town of Chatham and Bought on under the Eicon, in the said County of Kent, several Powers and Authorities tvere given, and certain Tolls granted, to the Trustees therein named, and by an Act, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the Amendment and Preservation of the Public Highways and Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, the said Acts were continued for the further Term of Five Years; and that by an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for continuing the Term, and varying the Powers of Two Acts, passed in the Third and Seventeenth " Years of his late Majesty King George the Second, for " repairing the Road from that Part of Chatham which " lies next to the City of Rochester, to Dunflan s

" Crop, near the City of Canterbury, in the County of " Kent, and for amending and widening the Road from " the present Turnpike Road, at or near a Place called " Makenade Comer, in the Parish of Pre/lon, to Bagham

" Crop and ShalmsfordLane-End, in the Parish of -

" ham, in the said County," several further Powers and Authorities were granted, and the Term of the said Acts was further continued, and that, the Term granted by the said last mentioned Act being now nearly expired, the said Roads cannot be kept in good and sufficient Repair, and safe and commodious for Travellers, unless the Term of the said Acts is further continued:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term, and to explain, amend, and extend, the Powers of the said several before-mentioned Acts, and that such further Order may be made in the Premises as to the House shall seem expedient.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty is concerned to acquaint the House of Commons, that His Endeavours to preserve Peace with Spain, and to adjust all Matters in Discussion with that Court, by an amicable Negotiation, have been rendered ineffectual, by an abrupt and Unprovoked Declaration of War on the Part of the Catholic King.

His Majesty, at the same Time that :He lincerely laments this Addition to the Calamities of War, already extending over so great a Part of Europe, has the Satisfaction to reflect, that nothing has been omitted on His Part, which could contribute to the Maintenance of Peace, on Grounds confident with the Honour of His Crown, and the Interests of His Dominions.

And He trusts, that, under the Protection of Divine Providence, the Firmncls and WilUom of His Parliament

Declaration Mr. Secretary Dundas prefehted to the House, by His Majesty's Command, tented. A Paper, intituled, " Declaration of War by the

" Court of Madrid against Great ."

And the Title of the said Paper was read.

The said Paper is as fqlloweth;

DECLARATION of War by the Court of Madrid against Great Britain.

One of the principal Motives which determined me to make Peace with the French Republic, as soon as its Government began to take a regular and solid Form, was the Conduct which England had observed towards me during the whole Course of the War, and the just Distrust which the Experience of Her ill Faith ought to occasion on my Part for the future. This ill Faith became manifest in the most critical Moment of the First Campaign, from the Manner in which Admiral Lord Hood treated my Fleet at Toulon, where he attended to nothing but the Destruction of what he could not carry away with him, and from hispresently after taking Possession of which Expedition

that Admiral concealed with the greatest Care from Don Juan de Langara, when they were together at 1 Toulon. The English Ministry afterwards confirmed the fame, from their Silence in all their Negotiations with other Powers, especially by the Treaty which was signed, the 19th November 1794, with the United States of America, without any Respect or Consideration for my Rights, which were well known to them: I noticed also that ill Faith in their Repugnance to adopt the Plans and ideas w'hich might accelerate the Conclusion of the War, and in the vague Answer Lord Grenville gave to my Amballador, the Marquis Del , when he applied for Succours to continue it: I was finally confirmed in that Opinion, by the Injustice with which they appropriated to themselves the valuable Cargo of the Spanijk re-captured Ship St. or , which they ought to have restored, according to the Agreement between my First Secretary of State, and of the DeJ'pacho the Prince De la Paz and Lord Saint Helens, His Britannic Majesty's Ambassador, and by the Detention of the Naval Stores coming for the Use of my Arsenals, on board Dutch Vessels, the forwarding of which w'as delayed under fresh Pretexts and Difficulties. Lastly, I had no Doubt left of the ill Faith in the Condmit of England, from the frequent Arrival of English Veil els on the Coast of Peru and to carry on a contraband Trade, and reconnoitre those Coasts, under the Pretext of the Whale Fishery, a Privilege they claimed by the Nootka Convention. Such, were the Proceedings of the English Ministry to prove the Friend-Ih ip, good. Understanding, and ft net Confidence which they had offered to observe with in all the Ope-

rations of the War, by virtue of the Convention of the 25th of May 1793. Since Peace wras concluded with the French Republic, I have not only had the best grounded Motives to suppose England harboured an Intention to attack my American Possessions, but I have received direeft Injuries, which have confirmed to me the Resolution formed by that Ministry, to oblige me to adopt a Part contrary to the Good of Humanity, torn to Pieces by the bloody War which is annihilating Vo ,. 52.

Europe, and contrary to the sincere Deftrc I have ma- .

.nifefted on repeated Occasions to put an End to it, by Means of Peace, proposing my good Offices to accelerate its Conclusion. England has in Fact fliewcd openly her View's against my Dominions, by the great Expeditions and Armaments lent to the Indies, dellined in part against St.Domingo, in order to impede its Delivery to France, as is evident from thfe Proclamations of the English Generals irt that Island, by the Establishment of trading Companies in North America, on the Banks of the River Mifouri, with an Intention to penetrate through those Regions to the South Sea; and lastly, by the Conquest she has just made on the Continent of South America, of the Colony and River of Demerari, belonging to the Dutch, which advantageous Situation puts her in the Way to occupy other important Points: But her View's have been still more hof-tilely and more clearly shewn, by her repeated Insults to my Flag, and by the Violence committed in the Mediterranean, by her Ships of War, in taking out of different Spanifi Vessels, the Recruits for my Armies, who were coming from Genoa to; by the

Atfts of Piracy and Vexation, by which the Corsican Privateers, protected by the Eng Government in the Island, destroy the Spanifi Trade in the Mediterranean, even within the Bays of the Coast of,

and by the Detention of several Spanish Vessels laden with Spanish Property, w'hich have been carried into the English Ports, under frivolous Pretexts, especially by the Embargo of the rich Cargo of the Spanish Ship Minerva, executed with Outrage to the Spanish Flag, and still detained in Spite of the most authentic Documents, shewing the said Cargo to be Spanifi Property, having been presented in the proper Court j the Offence has not been less grievous, which has been offered to the Character of my Ambassador Don Simon de las Casas, by One of the Courts of Law in London, u'hich ordered him to be arrested on the Ground of a Demand made by a Mailer of a Vessel, for a very small Sum of Money: And lastly, it has been no longer possible to tolerate the enormous Violations of the Spdnijk Territory on the Coasts of Alicant and Galicia, committed by the Brigs of the English Navy, the Cameleon and Kangurroo; and that which took place at the Island of Trinadad,was still more scandalous and insolent,

when Captain Vaughan, Commander of the Alarm Frigate, landed with Colours flying and Drums beating, at the Head of his whole Ship's Company, armed to attack the French, and revenge Injuries, which he said he had received, thus disturbing, by a Proceeding so offensive to my Sovereignty, the Tranquillity of the Inhabitants of that Island. By such reiterated and unheard of Insults, that ambitious Nation has repeated to the World, the Examples of her knowing no other Law' than that of the Aggrandizement of her Trade, by Means of an univerial Defpotism by Sea. She has gone beyond the Bounds of my Moderation and Forbearance, and obliges me, in order to support the Honour of my Crou-n, and to attend to the Protection I owe my Subjects, to declare War against the King of England, His Kingdoms and Subjects, and to command that such corresponding Orders betfent to all Parts of my Dominions, as may be best calculated for the Defence of my beloved Subjects, and for the Annoyance of the Enemy.

Ordered, That the said Paper do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Thomas Ridding, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Parish Church of Milbrooke, in the County of Southampton, and Diocese of Winchester,is a very ancient , Structure, and is in a very decayed and ruinous State and Condition, and not large enough for the Parishioners to assemble therein to hear Divine Service, and that it is necessary that the said Church should be taken down and re-built} and that the present Burying Ground or Church Yard is too small for the Use of the said Parish: That the Petitioners have agreed with Sir Charles Mill, Baronet, and his Undertenant, for a Piece or Parcel of Ground more convenient to re-build the said Church on, and which will also furnish an additional Piece of Ground for a Bi)-rying Place for the said Parish} and that it will be necessary for carrying the Purpol'es aforesaid into Execution, to raise a Sum of Money, which cannot be done without the Authority of Parliament.
