A Petition of th£ several Persons, whose Names ire thereunder signed, being a Quorum of the Commissioners of Sewers for the Tower Hamlets, was also presented to the House; and read; Setting forth; That; from Time immemorial, there have been various Sewers within the Tower Hamlets; in the County of dlesex, and under the Jurisdiction of certain Commissioners appointed from Time to Time for the Care of them; and that there are particularly in such DiUriel Two Sewers; one called the Man the Moon and flapping Level Sewer, which carries off great Quantities of Water from the City of London, and the several Parishes of Saint Botolph Aldgate, Saint Mary Whitechapel, Mile End New Town, Saint George's, Saint

John Wapping, and Saint Paul the other

Sewer is calicd the Nightingale Lane Sewer, which carries off great Quantities of Water from the several Parishes of Saint Mary Whitechapel, Saint Botolph Aid-gate, and Saint John Wapping, and such Waters are discharged therefrom by several Outlets into the lliver Thames-f and that; by Means of such Public Sewers, the Houses, Lands; Tenements, and Premisses, of the several Parishes aforesaid; and the Parts adjacent, are well and effectually drained; and that the Petitioners liaVe seen a Bill, now depending in the House, for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater and better Accommodation of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and it appears that such intended Docks, Cuts, and Basons, if carried into Executioil, will effectually cut off the Communication from such Sewers into the River Thames, and, if some other good and effectual Outlets are not made, the Waters of such Sewers will re Slow, become flagnate, and, it is greatly to be feared, lonie pestilential Disease would be the Consequence, and the forming new Sewers would be attended with very considerable Expence: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Provision may be made in such Bill for forming new Sewers at the Expense of the Persons applying for the said Bill; and that the same may be directed to be done under the Direction and Inspection of the Petitioners, and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, and Agents, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands, or that the Petitioners may have such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and the Petitioners are to be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill; against the said Petitions.

A Petition of the Commissioners of Sewers acting in and for the Limits of the Tower Hamlets, exclusive of Saint Catharine's and Blachzcall in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, from Time immemorial, there has been, and still is, a Common and Public Sciver, called the Tozver Hill Sewer, within the Limits and Jurisdiction of the said Commissioners, with which one of the principal Sewers of the City of London communicates; and that, at the latter End of the Year 1795, the said first-mentioned Sewer was blown up, which Accident was occasioned by a Deleft in the City of London's Sewers, and by an additional Quantity of Waters lately turned therein; and that the said Aril-mentioned Sewer was repaired, and Jias lately been again blown tip; and that, upon a careful Inspection of the same by skilful Surveyors, it appeared not to be sufficiently capacious to carry off the great Increase of Waters now flowing into the same ffom the said City Sewers, although large enough for the District to which it be longs; and that a riew Sewer of greater Capacity is thereby become necessary to be made; and that the District, within which the said first-mentioned Sewer is situate, is very small, and the making of such new 'Sewer will be attended with a very considerable Expence, which would fall extremely heavy on the Inhabitants; and that the Poor have ever since continued under the Management and Superintendence of the said Directors, who have been successively appointed according to the Provisions of the said Act, and who, as the Petitioners verily believe, have discharged the important Duties of their Office, not only with Uprightness and Integrity towards the incorporated Parishes by whom they have been severally conflicted, but with an humane Attention to the Comforts and Accommodation of the Poor, having rendered their House an Asylum for the Old and Infirm, a Place of useful Labour for such as are capable of Labour, and a Seminary of Inllruftion (as far as is needful) for the younger Branches committed to their Care; thus, by the System of Discipline introduced among them, inuring those, who before were subjected to no Discipline, to early Habits of Industry, and training them in the Ways of Piety and Virtue; and, from this Line of Conduct steadily pursued, the Petitioners look forward to the pleasing Prospect of seeing, in the more advanced Stages of their Establishment, many, who might otherwise have languished in Wretchedness, and have been the Outcasts of Society, become useful and valuable Members of the Community to which they belong, by being refeued at this critical Period from the baneful Contagion of Vice, and the fafeinating Se-duftions of evil Company; nor has the Attention of the Directors been confined solely to the Accommodation of that Part of the Poor, who, from having been received into the House, are the more immediate Ob-jests of their Inspection; they have also occasionally granted liberal Allowances to the Out-Poor, where Circumstances of particular and temporary Distress have rendered such Allowances expedient: Under the Influence of these Perfuafions, the Petitioners cannot but have observed with Regret the Progress of a Bill for the better Support and Maintenance of the Poor, by which the Salutary Regulations of their Act will be in a great Measure iuperfeded, the greater Part of their Buildings will be rendered useless, and their Rates for the Support and Maintenance of the Poor will be considerably increased, by the Creation of heavy Burthens in Addition to those which their present Establishment has necessarily produced; an Establishment founded upon the Faith of Parliament, pledged to them by an Act specially passed for that Purpose: And the Petitioners therefore implore the House to permit them to continue in the uninterrupted Enjoyment of the Powers which they now possess, by exempting them from the Operation of the said Bill (Ihould it pass into a Law) till at least both Experiments shall have been fairly tried, and Experience shall frith Certainty decide which is most practicable and expedient.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Tables until the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Consideration.

A Petition of Mark Noble, of the Parish of Lambeth, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner hath invented an Engine for raising Water, particularly useful on board Ships of War, and which have lately been adopted in the Service of His Majesty's Navy, for whose Use they were intended, and to whose Security the Petitioner conceives they will cffcntially contribute; and that His Majesty was. pleased, by Letters Patent, bearing Date the 29th of Vol. 52.

January 1784, to grant to the Petitioner the exclusive Right and Property, in his said Invention, for the Term of 14 Years; and that the Petitioner, having expended upwards of £. 3,000 in his Endeavour to obtain the Public Approbation of such Engines, was unable to introduce them into His Majesty's Navy until upwards of Eight Years of the Term of his Letters Patent had expired; so that, unless the Term granted to the Petitioner be prolonged, and the Property in the said Invention secured to him for an additional Term, the Petitioner cannot receive an adequate Recompence for his Labour, Expence, and Time, in bringing to Per-section his said Discovery: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for vesting in the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Af-ligns, the sole Use and Property of his said Invention, throughout the Kingdom of Great Britain, for such limited Time as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Charles Dundas, Sir liam Pulteney, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

and on Behalf of the Community of the said City, was referred; That-the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared, by an Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland in the Year 1693, That a Duty of Two Pennies Scots was granted to the Community of the City of Edinburgh, and to the Magistrates and Town Council of the lame, and their Successors, for the Uses therein specified, upon every Pint of Ale and Beer, either brewed, brought in, tapped, and fold, within the said Town and Suburbs, and Liberties thereof, which Duties were, by several Acts, made in the Third and Ninth Years of the Reign of King George the First, further continued and extended to the several Brewers within the Parishes of Saint Cuthbert,the Canongate, and South and North

Leith.

And it also appeared, by an Act of the Twenty-fifth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, That the said Rates, Duties, and Impositions, were continued for the further Term of Thirty-eight Years: — Then,

James Bruce, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Revenue granted by the said Acts, has been faithfully applied to the Purposes thereby directed, yet the same has greatly decreased lince the Commencement of the said Act of the Twenty-fifth of his late Majesty, info-much that in several Years the Gross Produce was not sufficient for Payment of the Interest of the Debt, far less for the Payment of the Annual Burthens; and although the Revenue, for some Years pall, has considerably increased, yet it is no Ways sufficient for Payment of the Debt contrafted upon the Credit of the said Duties, without a further Continuation of the Term already granted for collecting the fame, and that it will be necessary to explain and amend the said last mentioned Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act of the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for continuing the Duty of

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, Trustees, and Committee of the Parish of Saint George, in the County of Middlesex, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth. That, if the said Bill should pals into a Law, in its present Form, the Petitioners apprehend the Inhabitants of the said Parish will be more materially affected than any other Pari 111, within the same District, by the Regulation of the Rates and Taxes proposed to be levied under the Provisions of the said Bill; and that there are several other Parts of the said Bill, which, if passed into a Law, will be very prejudicial to the Interests of the Inhabitants of the said Parish: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against such Parts of the said Bill as affect the Interest of the Petitioners, and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour oi the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Trent and Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the llerga-of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were empowered to make a Navigable Canal, from the River Trbelow an ancient Ferry, called Wilden Ferry, in the County of Derby, to the River Mersey, at or near Runcorn Gap, in the County of Chester, which, by virtue of the said Alt, and another All passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, they have some Time lince completed; and that, by another All passed in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were also empowered to make another Navigable Canal, from the said first-mentioned Canal, on the South Side of Harecastle, in the County of Stafford, to Froghall, and a Railway from thence to ,which they have likewise completed; and that, by Surveys lately taken, it appears, that a Navigable Canal may be made, from and out of the said last mentioned Canal, at Froghall aforesaid, to or near Vttoxeter, in the said County of Stafford; and that another Navigable Canal may be made from, and out of, the said Canal, at Shelton, to or near Cobridge, in the said County, and another Navigable Canal, from and out of the said Trent and Mersey Canal, at Longport, to a Place called Dale Hall, in Burftem, in the said County; and also another Navigable Canal, from and out of the said Trent and Mersey Canal, at a Place called Sideway House, near Stoke upon Trent, to or near Lane End, in the said County of Stafford, which said last mentioned Canals will facilitate the Conveyance of Goods and Merchandize, and be of Public Utility; and that the Petitioners are willing and desirous, at their own Costs and Charges, to make, complete, and maintain the said several Canals, or Branches of Canal: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining the said several Canals, or Branches of Canal, on such Terms and Conditions, and with such Powers, Limitations, and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof} and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. William Egerton, Mr.

John Pitt, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Principal and Scholars of petition from

Hall and College of Brazen Nose, in the University of Bnuen Note Oxford, Patrons of the Rellory of Dunstan Step- ar imfLon-ney, in the County of Middlesex, and of the Reverend den Docks, Thomas Breithweitt, Dollor in Divinity, Rellor of the Parish of Stepney aforesaid, was presented to tire House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater

Accommodation

336 24° Februa A. 1797.

Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill should pass into a Law in its prefejit Form, the Petitioners apprehend they will be very much injured in their Rights and Interests: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by Counsel, against such Parts of the said Rill as affect their Rights and Interests, and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Rill, against the said Petition,

Kerry incio- A Petition of the Right honourable George Fdiyard lure Petition. Henry Arthur Earl of Lord of the Manor of

Kerry, in the County of Montgomery, and the humble Petition of the several other Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Lands and Te? nements within the said Manor, on Rehalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read , Setting forth. That thtre are, within the said

Manor, several Open Common and Waste Lands, belonging to the Petitioners, and others, which, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement, but it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Petitioners, and all other Persons interested therein, if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Allotments thereof made to them, according to their respective Rights and Interests therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Rill for effectuating the said several Purposes, in Rich Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Francis Lloyd and Sir Robert Williams Vaughan do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the King's Mef-House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to f:|gc respect-this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker of Specie, (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks it proper to communicate to the House of Commons, without Delay, the Measure adopted to obviate the Effects which might be occasioned by the unusual Demand of Specie lately made from different Parts of the Country on the Metropolis.

The peculiar Nature and Exigency of the same appeared to require, in the first instance, the Measure contained in the Order of Council, which His Majesty has directed to be laid before the House. In recommending this important Subject to the immediate and serious Attention of the House of Commons', His Majesty relies, with the utmost Confidence, on the experienced Wisdom and Firmness of His Parliament, for taking such Measures as may be best calculated to meet any temporary Pressure, and to call forth, in the moll effectual Manner, the extensive Resources of His Kingdoms, in support of their Public and Commercial Credit, and in Defence of their dearest Interests.

G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

Duke of Portland, Lord Grenville,

Marquis Cornwallis, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer,

UPON the Representation of the Chancellor of the Exchequer; Hating, That from the Result of the Information which he has received, and of the Enquiries which it has been his Duty to make respecting the Effect of the unusual Demands for Specie, that have been made upon the Metropolis, in Consequence of ill-founded, or exaggerated Alarms, in different Parts of the Country'; It appears, that unless some Measure is immediately taken, there may be reason to apprehend a Want of a sufficient Supply of Calli, to answer the Exigencies of the Public Service: It is the unanimous Opinion of the Board, That it is indispensably necessary for the Public Service, that the Directors of the Bank of England should forbear issuing any Calli in Payment, until the Sense of Parliament can be taken on that Subject, and the proper Measures adopted thereupon, for maintaining the Means of Circulation, and supporting the Public and Commercial Credit of the Kingdom, at this important Conjuncture. And it is ordered, That a Copy of this Minute be transmitted to the Directors of the Bank of England; and they are hereby required, on the Grounds of the Exigency of the Cafe, to conform thereto, until the Sense of Parliament can be taken as aforesaid.

(Signed) _ W. Fawkener.

A Petition of the Directors and Guardians of the Poor of the Parish of Stone, in the County of Staford, and of the Inhabitants and Land Owners of the faitl Towrt and Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, in the Year 1792, obtained an Act for providing a Workhouse for the Reception of the Poor of the said Parish, and for regulating and employing the Poor therein; and that, in the Purchase of the necessary Lands, in the Erection and Building of a proper and convenient Workhouse for the Reception of such Poor, and in Implements and Machinery, the Petitioners have expended near £.5,000; and that, by Means of this Establishment, the aged and infirm Poor have been comfortably provided for, the young trained up in Habits of Industry. Morality, and Decency, a Stop has been put to the great Abul'es that prevailed in the Parochial Expenditure, and those Poor, who laboured under temporary Distress or Disability, have been more liberally assisted and relieved in their own Dwellings than had before been found pradicable; and that, while the Poor themselves have derived these important Benefits from this Institution, the Petitioners have also been very considerably relieved from the heavy and growing Burthen of the Parochial Taxes; and that the Poor Rates for the said Parish have, ever since the Commencement of the Undertaking, been reduced upwards of One Third, and this very considerable Reduction has taken place notwithstanding a further Charge upon the said Rates for the Maintenance of the Families of Men serving in the Militia, and the Parochial Levies for the Army and Navy; and that the Petitioners are well convinced these combined and inestimable Advantages have arisen from the good Management of the Directors and Guardians appointed, under the Authority of the said Act; and that the Qualifications required have rendered these Directors and Guardians respectable, the Number of whom secured the Advantage of combined Judgment and due Deliberation, and effectually prevented the Abuse and Oppression of the Poor! That it is with deep Con cern the Petitioners apprehend that, by the Bill now depending in Parliament, the Management of Houses of Industry, and the Employment of the Poor therein, will be subjeded to such Regulations, Superintendence, and Controul, as will make void the Constitution and Establishment of the Directors and Guardians of the Poor of the said Parish (under whose Ma nagement the Iloyfe of Industry there hath so greatly flourished) and wholly set aside that Plan for the Maintenance, Education, and Employment of the Poor, from which so great Good hath been derived; and that the Consequences will be extremely injurious to the Petitioners, who, on the Faith of Parliament, have contracted so considerable a Debt by embarking in this Undertaking: That, by exempting Houses of Industry from the Operation of the intended Act, these evil Consequences will be avoided, and an Opportunity afforded of ascertaining, from fair Experiment, whether the Plan adopted by the Petitioners,' or that proposed by the said Act, be most practicable and expedient: And therefore praying, That a Clause, granting such Exemption to the House of Industry at Stone, may be introduced into, and form a Part of, the present Bill.

Ordered, That the faitl Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Support and Maintenance of the Poor was committed, be taken into further Couikleration.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Ralph He> on being examined, said. That a considerable Progress hath been made in amending the said Road, and a large Sum of Money hath been borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls by the said Acts granted and continued, Part whereof remains due and owing; and that the said Roads cannot be completely amended, widened, and kept in Repair, and the said Debt be discharged,unless the Terms of the said Acts are enlarged, and some additional Tolls granted; and it would be more convenient to the Trustees, and the said Roads be more effectually repaired, if the Powers and Provisions of the said Acts were repealed, and further and other Powers granted instead thereof.

And the Witness added, That the Highway leading from the North End of the Road above-mentioned, to the Turnpike Road from Alemouth to Hexham, in the said County of Northumberland, is narrow, incommodious, and in a ruinous Condition; and that if the same were properly amended, widened, and kept in Repair, it would open a short and ealy Communication between the said Two present Turnpike Roads, and be of Public Utility.

A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the better Support and Maintenance of the Poor; and Setting forth, That, in the last Session, an Act was obtained for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the several Parishes within the City of Lincoln and County of the same City, and of the Parish of Saint Margaret, Part whereof lies within the said Cify, and the other Part in the Close of Lincoln, in the County of Lincoln; and that the Petitioners were at the Expence of obtaining the fame, and the said Act is now in Execution, and, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, will be productive of the greatest Advantages to the Parishioners and Inhabitants of the several Parishes thereby united, will considerably reduce the Rates for the Relief of the Poor, who are very numerous and burthensome, and will also meliorate the Condition of the Poor themselves, who will be more comfortably maintained, instrufted, and supported, than they are at present; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive that the said Bill, if carried into a Law, will in ElFeft defeat the Execution of the said Act, which the Petitioners conceive is better adapted to the Circumstances of the Parishes united thereby, and will more effectu'

ally provide for,-and secure, the Relief, Instruction and Employment, of the Poor, than can be done by the Operation of the said Bill, should it be carried into a Law: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, unless Provision be made therein, so as wholly to exempt the Parishes united by the said Act from the Operations of the said Bill.

A Petition of the Directors of the Poor, within the Petition frot City of Lincoln and Liberties thereof, and also, of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, of Lincoln principal Parishioners and Inhabitants of the several againitthe Parishes within the City of Lincoln, and of the Parish of BlU" Saint Margaret in the Close, and City of Lincoln, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Parishioners and Inhabitants of the same Parishes, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice, of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners, after mature Consideration of the State of their Poor, and of what Measures might be the most likely to improve their Condition, and at the same Time relieve the Petitioners, in some Degree, from the Poor Rates, then very heavy and burthensome, did, in the last Session, apply for and obtain an Act for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the said several Parishes; and that the Directors of the Poor, elected under the said Act, have contrafted for the Purchase of certain Buildings and Premises intended to be enlarged and made commodious for the Reception of the Poor, and are further proceeding to carry into ElFeft the salutary Provisions of the said Act; and that the Petitioners are fully convinced that the said Act will be productive of the greatest Advantages to the Parishioners and Inhabitants of the said united Parishes, that it will tend greatly to reduce the Rates for the Relief of the Poor, and will, at the same Time, afford a more comfortable Maintenance for the Poor themselves, and introduce an efficient System for their better Instruction and Employment; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive that the said Bill, if carried into a Law, will militate against, if not wholly defeat, the good FurpofeS of the said Act: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, unless Provision be made therein, so as wholly to exempt the Petitioners from the Operations thereof.

A Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of Petition from the Poor of the Parish of Saint Leonard Shoreditch, in shoreditchT the County of Middlesex,on Behalf of themselves and against D the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was like- BllI‘ w'ife presented to the House, and read; Also taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That, if the same should pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend it will be injurious to, and materially affect, the Rights, Interests, and Properties of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, and tend very considerably to increase the Poors Rate, without being of Advantage to the really industrious or deserving Poor; and that the Petitioners conceive the Provisions, contained in the said Bill, are not calculated to effect the Purposes thereby intended, and will be the Means of defeating, and rendering ineffectual, many salutary Regulations now in Force within the said Parish, whereby the Poor are maintained, employed, and regulated, with the greatest Attention to their Accommodation and Relief; and that a Sum of £. 1,000, and upwards, has been expended in obtaining Acts for building the Workhouse,

£. 7,000 borrowed on Annuities for completing such Building, £. 2,000, and upwards, laid out in furnishing such House, erecting a Brewhoule and Bakehouse, and for proper Utensils and other necessary Expences: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel,.against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall leem meet.

Mr. Canning presented to the House, by His Majesty's Command,

Copy of a Treaty between His Britannick Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe Darmfladt, signed at Franc fort, the 1 oth Day of June 1796; and Transition.

And the Titles of the said Papers were reach

The said Copy is preferred amongst the other Papers of this Scliion; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

TRANSLATION of a Treaty between His Britannick Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe Darmfladt, signed at Francfort, the 10th Day of June 1796.

Be it known to those to whom it may concern, That His Majesty the King of Great Britain, and his Serene High nets the Landgrave of Hesse Darmfladt, in consideration of the Uriel Ties which unite Their Interests; and having judged, that in the present Situation of Affairs, it would contribute to the reciprocal Welfare of Great Britain, and of the Dominions of Hesse Darmfladt, to cement and strengthen, by a new Treaty of Alliance, the Connection which fublilts between them; His Britannick Majesty, in order to regulate the Ob-jests relative to this Treaty, has thought proper to nominate Charles Cravfurd, His Envoy at the Imperial and Royal Armies, and his Serene Highncls has nominated on his Part, for the same Purpose, the Baron Charles of Barckhaus, his Privy Councillor and Diivftor of the Council of War, who, being furnished with the necessary full Powers, have agreed to take for Balls of the present Treaty, the one formerly concluded between Great Britain and Hesse, the 5th of October 1793, to adopt such Parts of it as may be applicable to the present Circumstances, or to settle, by new Articles, those Points which it may be necessary to regulate otherwise 5 and as it is not possible to specify each particular Cafe, every Thing which shall appear to be determined in a precile Manner, either in the present Treaty, or in the former Treaty, shall be settled with Equity and good Faith, in conformity to the same Principles which have been adopted in the former Instances.

Article I.

There shall be therefore in virtue of this Treaty, between His Majesty the King of Great Britain and his Serene Highncls the Landgrave of Hesse Darmfladt, Their Heirs and Successors, a drift Friendship, and a linccre, firm, and constant Union, so that the one shall consider the Intcrcfls of the other as his own, and shall strive to promote them with good Faith as much as possible, and to prevent and remove all Dillurbance and Injury.

Article II.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, desiring to have in 1J is Service a Body of droops, to be employed wherever He may think proper, excepting in the East Indies, or on Board the Fleet; and his Serene Highncls wishing for nothing more than to give IJis Majesty this fresh tfroof of his Attachment, engages, by virtue of this Article, to let on Foot Three Battalions of Infantry, forming a Body of Two thousand Two hundred and Eighty-four Men, according to the annexed Specification. Thcfc Troops shall be ready to pais in Review before His Britannick Majesty's Commillary, the 14th Day of July, of the prclent Year, at Darmfladt, and to begin their March the following Day, for the Place of their Destination. The General whom His Britannick Majesty shall appoint Commander in Chief in the Countries where thele Troops shall serve, shall have Authority to employ them either together or in Detachments, and even to disperse them amongst the different Islands or Districts of his Command, in the Manner w'hich he shall judge the most advantageous for His Majesty's Service. well understood, that these Troops shall always remain under the immediate Orders of their own Chiefs. The said Corps shall consist of Men disciplined and exer-cil'ed, and well armed and equipped.

Article III.

In order to defray the Expences to which the Serene Landgrave shall be put for the Equipment of the said Corps of Troops, His Britannick Majesty promises to pay to his Serene Highness, for each Man, Thirty Crowns Banco, the Crown being reckoned at Fifty-three Sols of Holland,or at 4.J. 9 Money, of

which Payment shall be made immediately after the Review, and according to the effective State as shall then be verified. All the Camp Necessaries, as like wife all the Horses, Waggons, Draft Horses, Valets de Bat, and Waggoners, who may be necessary for the Troops, as well for transporting the Equipages, Provisions, Ammunition, Utensils, Sick, and other Objects of every Kind, as for the Field Pieces, with their Implements and Artillerymen, shall be furnished by His Britannick Majesty wherever they may be wanted.

Article IV. - *

Besides the Levy Money stipulated in the preceding Article, His Britannick Majesty shall cause to be paid to ever}' Officer, as also to every One employed, not a Fighting Man, of equal Rank, the Sum of Three Months Pay, according to his Rank, and upon the same Footing as his National Troops, in order to facilitate the Expence of his private Equipment; which Payment shall be made immediately after the Signature of the present Treaty.

Article V.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain engages Him-feIf in like Manner to pay to the Serene Landgrave, an Annual Subsidy, during the Six Yeats this Treaty is to continue. This Subsidy shall commence from the Day of the Signature, and it shall be paid at the Rate of Eighty thousand Crowns Banco per Annum. The Payment of this Subsidy shall be made regularly, without Abatement, every Quarter, to the Agent of his Highness in London.

Article VI.

These Troops shall remain in the Sendee, and at the Disposition of His Britannick Majesty, during Six Years; land His Majesty shall allow them, during this Term,

1. Every Thing that is necessary for their Subsistence, namely, Pay, Bread, Forage, and in general all Emoluments, as well ordinary as extraordinary, attached to every Rank, on the same Footing that he allows them to His British Troops, in the different Places of their Destination; and for this Purpose, the Statements of Payment shall be annexed to the present Treaty.

2. Medicines and Sustenance for the lick and wounded, with a Place, and the necessary Means of Conveyance, wherein they may be treated and taken Care of, precisely on the same Footing as the National British Troops, by their own Physicians and Surgeons.

The Pay shall commence from the Day of the Review, according to the effective State in which the said Corps shall be delivered, and which shall be verified by a Table, signed by the respective Ministers of the High contracting Parties, which shall have the same Force as if it had been inserted Word for Word in the present Treaty.

Article VII.

As in the before-mentioned Table, the Strength of each Company, of which Four make a Battalion, amounts to One hundred and Sixty-three Soldiers; it must be observed, that in this Number, are comprised Seven Men unarmed, intended, according to the established Custom in the Service, to serve as

Servants to Officers; and it is agreed upon, that these Men shall nevertheless pass Muller as Soldiers in every Respect.

Article VIII.

As it is to be feared, that notwithstanding all the Care made use of, it will not be possible entirely to prevent Desertion, until the Arrival of the Troops at the Place of Embarkation; and his Serene Highness promising to employ every Means in his Power, that the said Corps shall be embarked complete, it is agreed upon, that there shall be at the said Review, Ten lu-pernumerary Men per Company, to supply the Place of Deserters on the March, so that in cale, on the Arrival of the Corps at the Port, the Numbers of Supernumeraries shall exceed that of the Deserters, the Remainder may be distributed amongst the Battalions, and added to the Amount, in order to increasepin such Case, the Levy Money, Pay, &c.; and his Highness engages himself,1 moreover, to cause the said Corps to be escorted by a Detachment of Cavalry, in order to pick up Deserters, procure Quarters, &c. &c.: It being well understood, that the Expences, as Well of the March as of the Return of the Detachment of Cavalry, shall be defrayed by His Majesty.

Article IX.

All the Objects of Pay and Maintenance shall be calculated according to the Tableof the Annual Review, lb that the Vacancies happening from one Review to another, shall not make any Alteration in the State of Payment. His Majesty shall cause these Objects to be paid in Advance every Two Months, either by Assignments payable in Favour of the Hessian Commissioner, upon whatever Chest of His Majesty which may be nearest to the said Commissioner, or in ready Money, to his Serene Highness's Agent in London.

Article X.

A fresh Review shall take place regularly every Year. His Majesty shall give Three Months Notice of the Number of Recruits necessary to complete the Corps, which Number shall be fixed according to the Official Report of the First Day of , so that the Recruits shall be ready to be delivered to the Commis-

fary the First Day of July, at the Place of the First Review, or One Month after, at such Port in,

or at such Place on the Frontiers of the Empire, as His Majesty maj chuse for their Reception. The Term of their Delivery shall be deemed to be that of the new Review, and the Total of the Number of effective Men remaining, according to the Report of the Month of April, added to that of the Recruits delivered to the British Commissary, shall be considered as the effective State of the new Period, and shall not vary until the Review of the following Year.

Article XI.

There shall be paid for each Recruit, armed, equipped, disciplined, and exercised, the Sum of Twenty Crowns Banco, and his Highness the Landgrave takes upon himself the Expences of Transport to the Place of Embarkation, as well as of the Escort, which are to be reimbursed by His Britannick Majesty.

Article XII.

As during the Continuance of this Treaty, it will necessarily occur, that Officers or Soldiers, either for Family Reasons, on Account of Preferment, or for Sick-ness,will be obliged to return Home, His Majesty takes upon himself the Expences of their Transport in the Two former Cafes, as far as the Frontiers of the Empire, and in the latter, to their own Country. His Highness promises in Return to replace the Non-commissioned Officers and Soldiers, to whom he may give Penniflion to return (for any other Reason than that of Sickness) at his own/Expence, and without requiring the Consideration for Recruits fixed in the preceding Article, reserving to himself nothing but the Transport from the Frontiers of the Empire, unto the Place of their Destination. Moreover, his'Highness will never recal

an Officer or Soldier without urgent Cause, or without having acquainted 11 is Majesty thereof; and he will take Care that the Number of Officers shall be always complete.

Article XIII.

The most Serene Landgrave being at the Charge of furnithing the said Corps with Arms and Cloathing, in consequence of the Pay upon the Footing of English Troops, as agreed upon in thel'e Articles, His Majesty dial I cause iiidemnification to be made for such Loss only in Cloathing, Arm :, and Accoutrements, as shall be occasioned by tome Accident of War or of Voyage, as well as for every Expence incurred in the Transport of thel'e several Articles to the Troops, and all'o of every Thing the y may stand in Need of; it being well understood, that the aforesaid Articles tluill be delivered to the 'English Commillary at the same Time as the Recruits of the Year, in order that the same Vessel may convey both.

Article XIV.

In case an Officer should lole his Equipage, either on his Route, or by l'ome Accident in War, His Majesty shall grant him the same Indemnification as Eng-lijli Officers are allowed in similar Cafes.

Article XX *

His Britamick Majesty grants to his Highriefs the

Sum of'Fifteen thousand Pounds Sterling, to answer the First Expences of equipping this Corps, Payment of which shall be made immediately after the Signature of this Treaty, and shall be carried to the Account of Levy Money.

Article XXL _

Deserters shall be faithfully delivered Up on both Sides, and neither the Soldiers, nor any other Persons belonging to the Corps of shall be

permitted to settle in the Dominions of His Britannick Majesty.

In Witness whereof, we the undersigned, authorize ed by the full Power of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on one Side, and of his Serene Highness the lleigning Landgrave of HeJJe Darmjiadt on the other, have signed the present Treaty, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at Francfort, this Tenth of June One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six.

(L. S.) C. Craufurd,

Article XV.

As loon as his Serene Highness shall have put the Corps in a State to march within the Term agreed upon, he shall be considered as having fulfilled his Preliminary Engagements, so that the Payment of the Levy -Money, Subsidy, anil Pay, shall take place according to the aforesaid Determination, even in case His Majesty, on Account of l'ome unforeseen Event, should not think proper to have the Corps reviewed, or to cause it to march or embark.

_ Article XVI.

If before the Period of the Review, His Britannick Majesty shall find himself disposed to renounce this Treaty entirely, his Serene Highness shall receive, under the Title of Indemnification:

1 ft. The Levy Money.

2nd. The Equipage Money allowed to the Officers.

3rd. Three Months Pay for the Whole of the droops, according to the Table annexed to the Second Article, &c.

4th. One Year's Subsidy.

Article XVII.

At the End of Six Years His Britannick Majesty shall fend back the Corps, at the Dispolhl of his High-' ness, in the same State in which it was taken into His Service, and being at the entire Expence of transport -ing, until their Arrival at Darmjiadt. It being understood that His Majesty shall not pay the Levy Money for the Men who may be wanting at that Time, except in the same where he shall have failed to inform the Serene Landgrave of it Six Months beforehand, in order to save i.is Highness the Expence of a new Completion. If by Accident the Return should be retarded, the Treaty shall be tacitly prolonged, for One Year, in every Rupedt, and a certain Sum shall be agreed upon as an Equivalent for Levy Money, in proportion to the prclent Arrangement.

Article XVIII.

If His Majesty should think proper, after the Expiration of the Six Years fixed for the Duration of this Treaty, to keep the said Corps for some Years longer, his Highness consents to it beforehand, and it will be then only necessary to make an' Arrangement respecting the Levy and Equipage Money for the Officers, which will be calculated according to the Proportions of the present Treaty.

Article XIX.

H is Serene Highness reserves to himself the Jurisdiction over his Troops, as well as all Dilpositions respecting Promotion, Discipline, and interior Administration.

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman U flier of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's' Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Farmers, and Inhabitants in the County of Fife, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and of James An-derson, Tenant in Pitlochie, Prefes of a General Meeting of the Fife Farming Society, the Inverkeithing Farmer

Club, and other Farmers of the County of Fife, held at New Inn, in the said County, on the 3d of February 1797, w'as presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for regulating and converting the . Statute Labour, in the County of and for more effectually making and repairing the Highways within the said County; and Setting forth. That the same contains several Clauses which may materially affect the Interests of the Petitioners, particularly Clauses which authorize the Trustees to allocate, in the Manner therein mentioned, the Statute Labour or Services to the Turnpike Roads, by which the Cross or Bye Roads may become impafiable, as also sundry other Clauses, whereby the Trustees are empowered to rate (possessed by themselves) Land by the Rent or Extent, in their own Option, without allowing the Tenant the like Option, to rate Plantations by Rent instead of Extent, to afiefs Cottagers and all Tradesmen to the Value of Six Days Labour, to allow the Proprietor, possessing his own Lands, to rate himself, instead of subjecting him to have his Ploughgates rated by the Surveyors Lift, whereby these may be greatly undervalued, to regulate the Conversion of Victual, where the Rent is payable in Grain, in a Manner different from the County Fiars, to allow summary Diligence at the Instance of the Pro-

prietor against the Tenant, without Citation of Party, and being heard in his own Defence, to allow the Heritor Payment for his Ground for widening Roads, without giving a Deduction to the Tenants from their Rents, when Ground, for a similar Purpose, is taken from them, to make a Distinction as to the Height of Houses situated in the Line u'here the Road may happen to pals, so as to preserve those of a certain Height, while Houses below Twelve Feet are liable to be pulled down, and to deny a Right of Appeal to the Court of Session, where the Party thinks himself aggrieved:

Against which Clauses, and all other Parts of the said Bill, which may tend to their Injury or Prejudice, the Petitioners pray. That they may have Leave to be heard by themselves or Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against; the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Ward of 5/7-Hngfgate, in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth, That the said Bill will, if carried into Execution, materially injure the Petitioners, and the several Parishes within the said Ward, from a Reduction in the Receipt of the several Parliamentary and Parochial Assessments, by a Deterioration of the Houses and Warehouses within the said Ward, and in particular the same will very materially injure the Property of such Houses and Warehouses; and, upon these Grounds, tfea -Petitioners submit that the same ought 9

Scheme altogether, or they would have prefaced the Attempt of succeeding in it by an upright and honourable Pledge of complete Indemnification; and the Petitioners have, with Anxiety, but with Patience, waited for this Avowal, of liberal Integrity, this Earnest indeed of im-. mediate and iiridt Equity on the Part of the Supporters of the Wet Dock System, and having trailed such Sentiments would have dictated their Conduit, the Petitioners have relied in confident Silence, but they now learn with Sorrow that not only the Bill is pursued with increased Assiduity, but- that Compenfiuion to the various Claimants has not yet been agreed upon; the Petitioners then once again iolicitcufly entreat the Protection of the House, recalling its Attention to the Cale of the numerous Individuals who will leriously suffer if this Measure is determined upon, many will have to regret the total Loss of immenle Property, but a much larger Proportion (whole Condition no Indemnity in the Power of a Wet Dock Corporation to offer will be competent to remedy) must be driven from their Employments and natural Occupations; among the latter Description of Sufferers, they beg Leave to notice the Body oF Lightermen and Watermen who reside in the said Ward, and who form lo elfential, lb important a Nurlery for those brave Seamen who man the Bulwark of the Nation; if however the urgent Appeals of those Individuals, apprehensive of Ruin and Annihilation to their Properties and Livelihoods, offered in Temperance and Moderation, should in the Wisdom of the House be thought of less Avail and Consideration than the pre fling Solicitations of other Individuals who plead for Sanction to an immediate and direct Removal of the Trade of London from its ancient Seat and Boundaries, under Colour and Pretence of benefiting it, then indeed they must, with Deference to the Will and Judgment of the Commons of Great Britain, in Distreis, submit, but, if the National Good hereafter should ultimately require (which

Mr. Douglas reported from the Committee, That they had come to several llefolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will jpleafe to receive the same.

Mr. Douglas accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Rei'olutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient, for the more general and speedy Promulgation of the Laws, that His Majesty's Printer (instead of printing the 1,126 Copies of such of the Public Statutes of the Realm as are now printed by him at His Majesty's Expence) should be authorized and directed to print not less than 3,550 Copies of every Public General Statute, 200 Copies of every Public Local Statute (including Road Acts) and 200 Copies of each Private Statute; which it appears, from the Statements contained in the Report referred to this Committee, may be done without any additional Expence to the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer should be authorized and directed to print and deliver (or transmit by Post) as soon as possible, after each Bill has received the Royal Assent, the aforesaid Number of 3,550 Copies of each Public General Statute, according to a certain Mode of Distribution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer should be authorized and directed to print and deliver, or transmit in like Manner, the aforesaid 200 Copies of each Public, Local, and Private Statute, according to a certain Mode of Distribution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Chief Magistrate, and Head Officer, of any City, Borough, or Town Corporate, in England and Wales, and of every Royal Burgh in Scotland, and every Sheriff, Clerk of the Peace, and Town Clerk, receiving any such Copies, should preserve them for the Public Use, and transmit them to his Successor in Office.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of effectuating the Promulgation of Private Statutes, and also of ensuring an adequate Compensation to the Clerk of the Parlia-f mciit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer should also be authorized and directed, to class the General Statutes and the Special Statutes (viz. the Public, Local, and Private Acts) of each Session in separate Volumes, and to number the Chapters of each Class fepaTately, and alto to print One General Title to each Volume, together with a General Table of all the Acts passed in that Session.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the precise Duration of every new temporary Law should be expressed in the Title of the Bill, and also in a distinct Clause at the End of the Bill, and no where else.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, where the Revival of several Expired Statutes, or the Continuance of several Expiring Statutes, is proposed, all such as are to be revived should be included in one Bill; and such as are to be continued in another: And that every Bill, presented for the Revival of several Statutes, or for the Continuance of several Statutes, should express in its Title, that the same is for reviving, or for continuing, the several Statutes therein mentioned; and should describe in its Title every such Statute by its Year, Chapter, and Day of passing; together with the precile Duration proposed to be given thereto.

George Goodenough, Esquire, Secretary to the Tax

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Richard Wooding being examined, said. That in pursuance of the said Act, Three Stone Bridges have been erected by the Undertakers, between Whitney and Clifford, in the Course of about Twelve Years, at an Expence of upwards of £. 5,000, all of which have fallen down, owing solely to the Badness of the Foundation in the Bed of the River for erecting a Stone Bridge, which has been a great Loss to the Undertakers, and of much Inconvenience to the Public.

That if a Bridge was built of Timber and Stone, it might be done with every Probability of its being permanent, and more suitable to the Bed of the River, and of equal Convenience to the Public; and which the Petitioners Thomas Longfellow, John Longfellow, and John Phillips, are willing to undertake, in case the Act is amended and altered, and the Tolls thereof varied from the present Act.

A Petition of Thomas Rozvcroft, of the City of Lon- Mr. Ro . don, Merchant, was presented to the House, and read; tion'a nit Setting forth. That the Petitioner is the Owner and London Occupier of a certain public Sufferance Wharf, called gjifks'&c Hubbert's Wharf, adjoining to Cherry Garden, in the Parish of Saint Mary Magdalen, Bin the County of Surrey, and also of certain extensive commodious and substantial Warehouses erected there, and used with the said Wharf; and that the Business of a Public Sufferance Wharfinger has for many Years past been carried on with Credit and Advantage at the said Wharf and Premises, and the Petitioner, relying on such Business not only continuing, but increasing, has, from Time to Time, expended very considerable Sums in the Purchase and Improvement of the said Premises; and that the said Wharf, Warehouses, and Piemiles, are well calculated for landing, shipping, and housing. Foreign and other Merchandize, for accommodating the Merchants of London and Southwark, for securing and protecting the Public Revenue, and for discharging all other Duties appertaining to legal Quays at the Port of London; and that a Bill for making Wet Docks, Balons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, is now depending in the House, which Bill, if pasted into a Law, will greatly injure, if not wholly annihilate, the Business carried on at the Petitioner's said Wharf and Premises, and consequently render them of very inconsiderable Value, if some Provisions, at present omitted, are not thereby, or otherwise, secured to the Petitioner; and that the said Bill is in other Respects injurious to him: And therefore praying to be heard, by himself, his Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, at the Bar of the House, or otherwise, and to offer Clauses for Compensation and Indemnity, or the Grant of Privileges limilar to those which the intended Dock Company are soliciting, in regard to the landing, shipping, and discharging of Foreign and other Goods, and for such other Relief as Parliament may think the Petitioner entitled to, and also to offer such Proofs and Arguments, in Opposition to the said Bill, in its present Form, as he shall be advised.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by himself, his Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an lnftrubtion to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Prisoners confined for Debt in His Majesty's Ptifon of the King's Bench, was presented to the House, and read; Complaining of their Did refs; and Setting forth. That the Allowance to Insolvent Debtors by the Laws in being, from the great Increase in the Price of Provisions, is inadequate to their Support: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and not only to extend the Act of the Second of King George the Second, by making the Debtor's Weekly Allowance, adequate to his Support, according to the present Price of the Necessaries of Life, but by enlarging the Sum, so that Debtors of every Description may take the Benefit of it, to which they conceive themselves in ftrid Justice equally entitled.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Crozedy being examined, said, That the Poor belonging to the said Parishes, Hamlets, and Town-ships, are become very numerous, and are supported at a very great Expence to the Inhabitants thereof; that it is apprehended, if a proper and suitable House were provided for the Reception of all the Poor within the said Parishes, Hamlets, and Townships generally, and proper Powers were given for their Regulation, Employment, and Government, it would not only be a great Advantage to.all Persons paying to the Poor Rates of the said Parishes, Hamlets, and Townships, but would also tend to the better Relief and Comfort of the Poor themselves.

provided the Surveyor for the Crown would swear to his Survey, the Officers and Ministers of the Crown now acting coileftively, after' ma-' ture Deliberation, persisted in requiring unconditional Submission to their illegal unqualified Demand, in direct - Violation of their Duty, and in open Contempt of the most lacred Privilege of Parliament: On further Inquiry, fthe Petitioner was informed, that the Instances of such Injustice were numerous, and that the Officers and Ministers of the Crown had made great Progress in establishing a System of Double Taxation by making arbitrary Additions to the Taxes regularly imposed by Parliament; that such Stretches of Power had been chiefly exercised against those who had become obnoxious to the Officers and Ministers of the Crown, by faithfully discharging a severe Duty in refilling arbitrary Ministerial Encroachments on the Prerogative of the Crown and the most lacred Privileges of Parliament: That, in Consideration of enormous Advantages unjustly obtained from a partial System of Finance, many had entered into tacit or express Combinations to support the System of Double Taxation, that a great Number had yielded from the Dread of Adversaries armed with all the Power of the State, the Influence of the Crown, and the still more exorbitant Authority derived from the Administration of a new and impracticable System of Finance, professing to pay the Public Creditors at the enormous Rate of Eighty Cent, more than was borrowed, and that those who had dared to apply for Redress were constantly baffled by the Intrigues of Office, Ihifting Responsibility from Department to Department, a Practice in which from long Experience they had become exceedingly dexterous: Of this Class is the Petitioner, who for many Years has suffered under a violent Ministerial Perfection, while, by the highest Command, he has been deeply engaged in a'most laborious and expensive In-veftigation concerning the Means of preserving those brave Men who are so eminently distinguished by their Valour and Perseverance, whose unparalleled Atchieve-ments dart a Gleam of Hope through the Gloom in which the Civil Departments are unhappily involved, and who are inhumanly sacrificed by a barbarous Opposition of the Officers and Ministers of the Crown to the Means by which Myriads of Lives might with Certainty have been laved, as has actually been demonstrated, in the Army, in the Navy, in the Militia, and in the Service of the East India Company, in AJia, Africa, and America, as can be proved by authentic official Vouchers: Yet this Plan, after much Intrigue, has at length been fatally suppressed by a gross Violation of the Royal Prerogative, to the Bane of the Army and Navy, and the Triumph and Exultation of a dangerous Enemy, by whom it has been eagerly adopted, and to whole Success it has eminently contributed. To give a plausible Colour to an unjust, impolitic, and impracticable System of Finance, to which Honour, Humanity, and found political (Economy, have been sacrificed, the Officers and Ministers of the Crown obstinately persist in enforcing Double Taxation, and their arbitrary Exactions are only bounded by the Apprehension of rousing the just Constitutional Jcalously of Parliament, and compelling the House to withdraw that Confidence with which Ministers have long been indulged, beyond all former Example: The §.

Applications of the Petitioner to the Surveyor for the Crown, to the Collector, and to the Commissioners of Appeal, were insolently repelled, and he has been reduced to the severe Alternative of abandoning his Duty, and becoming legally obnoxious to the just Indignation of Parliament, or fullering himself to be plundered, his House, the boasted Cattle of a Subject, through which the Winds and Storms might blow but despotic Power could not enter, to be converted into a Scene of Desolation, Riot, and Confusion, and his Character to be profaned as a public Defaulter: His Property was carried off' with distinguished Marks of Contempt and Derision, without the Option of redeeming it, and, after a pretended Sale, he was insulted by a mock Tender, contumeliously held out as the Balance accruing from a Property of more than Ten Times the Value of the illegal Demand: The Officers and Ministers of the Crown Hand alone responsible for these atrocious Crimes, committed at a melancholy Period, and under afflicting Circumstances, which renJ der it abl'olutely impossible for them to l'creen themselves, with their usual Tricaflery, behind the Sanctuary of the Throne. On an Appeal to the Treasury Board, and a Reference from that Board to the lax Office, the Demand was acknowledged to have been from the Begininng illegal, and the Tax on the Windows of the House was reduced to Half the Sum for which Twenty Times the Value had been confiscated: But no Recti-tution has been offered, nor any Atonement for sacri-legiously removing the Land Marks of the Constitution, and impiously violating the most sacred Privilege of Parliament; on the contrary, further illegal Demands are continually made on the Petitioner, he is insultingly interrogated, if he is not now satisfied, when the Demand is mercifully reduced to Half the Sum for which his Property was confiscated, and his House is Annually entered, and his Property seized, by a law-lcfs Banditti, acting under the outward Forms and pretended Authority of Law: The Crimes of the Ministers of the Crown are also highly aggravated by endeavouring to draw this Cause into a Court of Law, which, as involving the highest Privilege of Parliament, is only cognizable in the House of Commons, as the Petitioner is instrufted, by numerous Precedents and Resolutions, and particularly by a solemn Resolution of the House, voted 28th January 1688, and afterwards adopted by the Upper House of Parliament, "That " King James II. by the Assistance of evil Councillors, " judges, and Ministers, employed by him, did endeavour to subject and extirpate the Laws and Liberties of this Kingdom, by sundry Means, l'uch as " by Prosecutions in the Court of King's Bench for " Matters only cognizable in Parliament.anddiversother " arbitrary Measures." Another Aggravation yet remains, for the arbitrary Courses of the Officers and Ministers of the Crown exceed all former Bounds of Li-centioufness, they have withheld a Petition from Parliament in which these Fasts were stated, presented falle Accounts, including Money thus arbitrarily and illegally levied by a criminal Aggression on private Property, and a bold Invasion of Privilege, as a fair Return of Taxes regularly granted by Parliament, and thus fraudulently obtained a false Report of the actual Receipt and probable future Produce of the Revenue: Left therefore, as in the last Appointment of a Committee in the Year 1792, to enquire into, and report, the actual Receipt and probable future Produce of the Revenue, the Committee now appointed should not have sufficient Information to enable them to make a true and satisfactory Report, the Petitioner humbly prays, that this Petition may be referred to that Committee to examine and report, or that the House may adopt such other Measures as their Wifiriom may direct, to vindicate the Privilege of Parliament, and its inseperable Concomitants, the Prerogative of the Crown, and the Inviolability of Property, from the Encroachments

Fishery, and that without an Extension of the said Act, there will be a considerable Decrease in the Fishery, That the said Fishery has much suffered, and is under particular Difficulties from the Circumstances of the War, and if it should be so much further oppressed, that any of the Seins, or Concerns, should be given up, from the present Difficulties, it would not be easy in future Times to re-establish them, beneficial as they are to the Country, and absolutely necessary for the County of Cornwall in particular, both for Employment of one Body of Men, and affording Food to another.

Crinda Farm, to, or near to, Bridge, in the County of Monmouth, whereby certain Persons were united into a Company called " The Company of Proprietors of the Monmouthshire Canal Navigation," who were, by the said Act, empowered to raise amongst themselves £. 120,000, for carrying the same into Execution, and also a further Sum of £.60,000 by Mortgage, if the same should be necessary; and that a certain Pool or natural Bason, called The Fill, adjoining the Town of Newport, was the Spot pointed out in the Plan delivered, previous to the passing of the said Act, as the properest Place for the Bason of the Canal, on the South Side of which Pill are the above-mentioned lands, called The Waterjide or Cinder hill Wharf, and The Friars Fields, in which tire Petitioner is interested as aforesaid; and that tire Company have made an imperfect and partial Bason on the North Side of, and close 'to, the said Pill, by which Means the Petitioner is excluded from deriving any Benefit from the Wharfage or Tonnage of the Navigation, and the Wharfs adjoining are insufficient for the Trade on the Canal; and that the said Company, at a General Half Yearly Assembly, held in October last, approved and ratified an Agreement which their Sub-Committee had previously entered into with the Petitioner, on Behalf of himself and others, for extending the Canal acrols the said Pill into the adjacent Lands on the South Side of the said Pill, and no further; and that a Bill has been brought into the House for enabling the said Company of Proprietors to extend the said Canal, from its present Termination, across the said Pill, through and beyond the above-mentioned Lands, to the Extent of a Mile and a Half from the present Limits of the Canal, and also for enabling the Company to raise an additional Sum for completing their original Undertaking, and for extending the Canal, and for other Purposes in the said Act mentioned; and the Petitioner begs Leave to state, that the Bason of the said Canal ought to be made in the said Pill, according to the origins!Intention

of the said Act, and that the said Agreement should be carried into Execution, which would be of the greatest Utility to the Public, and to the general Concern of the Canal; and that, if the said Bill should paf's into a Law in its present Form, it will, in many Respects, be highly injurious to the Petitioner and his Property, and the proposed further Extension of the Canal can answer no possible Purpose of Utility to the Public, or to the Proprietors of the Canal in general: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by himself, his Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for extending the Monmouthshire Canal Navigation,.and for explaining and amending an Act, passed in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal, be read a Second Time.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole Iloufc, to whom the Bill for confirming and continuing, for a Time to be limited, the Restriction, contained in the Minute of Council of the 26th of February laid, on Payments of Cash by the Bank, was again re-committed, with respect to several other Clauses which, upon Friday last, were offered to be added, by the House, to the Bill; That the Committee had added several other Clauses to the Bill, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Clauses, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were Twice read; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, That nothing therein contained should extend to any Cafe, where the Persons required to be held to Special Bail, shall not make an Affidavit, that they have in their Custody or Power Money in Calb equal to the Whole, or Three-fourths of the Debt, for which such Special Bail is required.

And the Question being put, That the said Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, declaring, That the Restraint laid by this Act on the Bank as to issuing Cash, shall not have any Force or Effect, unless the Governor and Company shall, within after the Bill is passed by the House of Commons, signify in Writing to the Speaker, to be communicated to the House, and entered on the Journals, that it is the Desire of the Governor and Company, that such Restraint should be continued for the Whole of the Time mentioned in the Bill, or for any shorter Time to be mentioned in such Notice.

And the Question being put, That the said Clause be brought up;

The House divided.

Petition of Duke of Portland, &c. against the Bill for equalizing the County Rrtte for Miildle/ex.

A Petition of the most Noble William Henry Cavendish Bent inch, Duke of Portland, the most Noble George Rowlett, Marquis of Winchester, and the Right honourable

Charles Cocks, Lord Sommers, and the humble Petition of the LandOwners, Proprietors, Vestrymen, and House-hoklers, of the Parish of SaMary-le-Bone, on Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for empowering the Justices of the Peace, for the County of Middlesex, at their General or Quarter Sessions of the

Peace, to make a fair and equal County Rate for the said County; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners,' feeling themselves much aggrieved and injured in their respective Properties, should this Attempt be crowned with Success, and the said Bill carried into a Law, beg Leave to represent, that its Object is of the most novel and alarming Nature, and tends to subvert all those ancient Quotas of Contribution to the County Rate of Middlesex, which have been established by ancient Custom, and have been finally fixed by the Legislature of this Country since the Twelfth Ytfar of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second; and that the Petitioners, having purchased their Estates, and expended considerable Sums of Money in the Improvement of these Estates by modern Buildings, under the Faith of Parliament, would be greatly injured, and the Inhabitants of other Parishes proportionably alleviated, at their Expence, in their future Assessments, by this equalizing Syltern of Property, founded on the vilionary Bails of Equity, in Opposition to subsisting Law, and the genuine Principles of the Eng/ijhConftitution: What lleafon can

be assigned for changing the County Rate of sex alone, while all other Counties preserve their ancient Rates in their ancient and unequal Form ? If so important a. Change be made in one County, it should be also adopted in all: The Realon that applies to the County Rate attaches also on the Land Tax of the Kingdom, and affects all the Landed Interest of Great Britain: And the Petitioners therefore object to the Principle of this Bill as a dangerous Innovation, and for those, and various other lleafons which may be alledged against it, pray the House, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, if they think fit and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second Time upon Wednesday Morning next.

cils and Assemblies of the said Plantations, to adopt such Measures as shall appear to them Left calculated to obviate the Caules which have hitherto impeded the natural Increase of the Negroes already in the Islands, gradually to diminish the Neceftity of the Slave Trade, and ultimately to lead to its complete Termination; and particularly, with a View to the same Elfect, to employ such Means as may conduce to the Moral and Religious Improvement of the Negroes, and secure to them, throughout all the British West India Islands, the certain, immediate, and active Protection of the Law; and at the same Time alluring His Majesty, that this House will concur in such Measures as shall appear requisite to be taken by this House for the Attainment of the same Object;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Borough of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to regulate the Trial of Caules and Indictments, which, arise within the Limits of certain Cities and Towns Corporate within this Kingdom; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive there are divers Clauses and Provisions contained therein which will materially affect their Rights and Privileges, and be highly prejudicial and inconvenient, and attended with great Expence to the Inhabitants of the said Borough, if the same should pass into a Law in its pretent Form, and will be destructive of the Peace, Order, and good Government of the Town, and may diicourage Persons from protecting Offences committed within the Borough: And therefore praying, That the said Bill, in its present Form, may not pats into a Law; and that the Borough and down of Great Yarmouth may be particularly excepted out of it, and that the Petitioners may be at Liberty to be heard, by themselves, their Countel, or Agents, against such Parts of the said Bill as are prejudicial to the Interest and ancient Rights and Privileges of the said Borough.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

An ACCOUNT of the Sum granted out of the Consolidated Fund, for the Service of the

Year 1796; and the Produce to satisfy the fame.

The Sum granted out of the Consolidated Fund, for the Service of the Year 1796, amounts to Three Million Five hundred thousand Pounds; but that Fund has not hitherto produced sufficient to satisfy any Part of the fame.
