John Smyth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to H is Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved,. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Five Millions, be granted to His Majesty, towards defraying the Expences and preventing the Increase of the Debt of His Majesty's Navy, for the Year 1797.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, net exceeding One Million One hundred and den thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to pay ctf and discharge the Exchequer Bills which have been issued in pursuance of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for " enabling His Majesty to railc the Sum of Two Millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, for the Uses " and Purposes therein mentioned."

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One Million Three hundred and Seventy thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to pay eft' and discharge the Exchequer Bills which have been issued on the Credit of the growing Produce of the Consolidated Fund, for the Service of the Year 1796.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two Millions One hundred and Seventy-seven thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the Sum of Three Millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, charged by an Act of the last Session of Parliament on the Consolidated Fund, for the Service of the Year 1796.

Memorandum:

Notices were again sent to the Parties, with Orders for their Attendance accordingly.

Sir John Sinclair reported from the Committee appointed to take into Consideration the Means of promoting the Cultivation and Improvement of the Waste, Uninclosed, and Unproductive Lands, and the Common Arable Fields, Common Meadows, and Common of Failure, in this Kingdom, and who were empowered to report their Proceedings, together with their Opinion thereon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with several Resolutions, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table; Where the Report was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Cultivation and Improvement of the Waste, Uninclosed, and Unproductive Lands, and of the Common Arable Fields, Common Meadows, and Common of Pasture, in this Kingdom, is an Object of such efl'ential Consequence to the general Interests of the Nation, that every Means ought to be adopted speedily and effectually to accompli fit the fame, and that every possible Step ought to be taken for that Purpose in the Course of the present Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it would tend to promote the Inclosure of such Lands, if a Bill were passed for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Waste Lands, Commons, Common Fields, and other Commonable Lands, of that Part of Great Britain called England, by Agreement among the Parties interested therein, and for removing any legal Disabilities which may Hand in the Way of such Agreement.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it would materially tend to the' Inclosure of such Lands (more especially where the Parties are neither numerous or complicated) if, in Cafes where the Parties are not unanimous, a" Law were passed for ena-

bling any Person or Persons, entitled to any Waste, Uninclosed, and Unproductive Lands, Common Arable Fields, Common Meadows, or Common of Pasture, or any Portion thereof, in that Part of Great Britain called England, to divide, inclose, and hold the same in Severalty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Chairman do move the House for Leave to bring in a Bill, or Bills, pursuant to the above Resolutions.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report, with the Appendix, be printed.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon IVednc Morning next.

The said Report is preservd amongst the other Papers of this Session.

N. B. A printed Copy is with the Original.

and the Petitioners are adviled, that, under this Clause, it is competent to the House, and to the Legislature, to relieve the Petitioners from the heavy Grievances under which they labour, either by diminishing the Duty now impoled in the Lowland District, or by raising the Duty imposed on Stills in the Highland District: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their serious Consideration, to give the Petitioners such Relief as may seem just, and to allow the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of the Matter contained in this Petition.

A Petition of the Prisoners (in Number 210) confined for Debt in His Majesty's Gaol of Newgate, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a considerable Number of the Petitioners have been confined in this Prison from Three to Four Years, with l'carcely any Thing but the Gaol Allowance to lubfift upon, to the great Detriment of their Healths, and Ruin of their Families; and that, without the Interference of the House, the Petitioners have the gloomy Profpcd of perpetual Imprisonment before their Eyes, and as this Prison, in particular, is at present lo crowded, that there are from 15 to 25 Persons confined in One Room, comparatively small, they consequently have every Thing to fear from Epidemic Diseases: And there-

fore praying the House to take their distrelfing same into immediate Consideration, and that some Mode of Relief may be granted, under such Regulations and Restrictions as the Necessity of their same requires, and to the House shall seem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

are thereunto subscribed, was referred j That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was readj and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, James , Taylor, Esquire, Deputy' Clerk of the Peace for the County of Lancaster, being examined, said, That the Sessions in the said County are Quarterly held in Four Sub-divisions, at which it is usual that the Justices of the Peace only attend who reside in their respective Districts; and the Justices finding, that when they acted in the Business that concerned the County at large (in which they had all an equal and concurrent Jurisdiction) it was expedient they should be assembled together, did appoint, some Years past, that an Annual Session should be held in a central Part of the County, at which the auditing the Treasurer's Accounts, the appointing of Officers in the Nomination of Justices of the Peace, who are paid out of the County Rates, and the discharging of all Business that related to the County at large, flhould be transacted: That the said Session was held for many Years to the Satisfaction and Advantage of the County, but it hath been lately found, that it is liable to be disturbed, and the Establishment of the Annual Session cannot be supported without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for obviating and removing Doubts respecting the Holding of the Adjournments of the General Courts of Quart er Sessions of the Peace in and for me County Palatine of Lancaster, and for authorizing the Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the said County, to hold an Annual General Sessions, and also a Special Sessions, for the Purposes therein mentioned: And that Mr.

Stanley and Mr. Blackburne do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

GEORGER.

His Majesty, having agreed to a Marriage proposed between the Princess Royal and the Hereditary Prince of IVirtembergh, has thought fit to communicate the same to this House. His Majesty is fully persuaded that this Alliance with a Protestant Prince, lo considerable in Rank and Station, and who is connected with His Majesty's Royal Family, by their common Delcent from the Princess Sophia of Hanover, cannot but be acceptable to all His faithful Subjects; and the many Proofs which He has received of the affectionate Attachment of this House to His Person and Family, leave Him no Room to doubt of the Concurrence and Assistance of this House, in enabling Him to give such a Portion to His elcieft Daughter as maybe Ratable to the Honour and Dignity of the Crown.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgess, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was prclented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to regulate the Trial of Causes and Indictments, which arile within the Limits of certain Cities and Towns Corporate within this Kingdom; and Setting forth, That, if the Civil and Criminal Jurisdiction of the said City should undergo the Change proposed, the Traders and Inhabitants thereof will be greatly injured and opprelLd, the good Laws, Orders, and Conilitutions for the Preservation of the Rivers and Port will be diRegarded, and the City of Bristol become a Scene of Riot, Disorder, and Depreciation, and not a City of good Government: And therefore praying, That the City and County of Bristol may be wholly exempted from4 the Provisions of the said Bill, or that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel or Agents, against so much thereof as may affect the said City and County, and the Traders and other Inhabitants thereof.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Common-ally eft the incorporated Society of Merchant Venturers in the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also prdented to the House, and read; Likewise taking

.Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are under very great Apprehensions of the mischievous consequences of the said Bill, for that, if the same lliould pals into a Law, Actions for Causes, arising within the County of the City of Bristol, may be tried at the Instance of either Plaintiff or Defendant by a jury of the County of Somerset, at a great Di(lance from Bristol, whereby a considerable additional Expence will be incurred by the Traders and other Inhabitants of that large and populous City, in taking their Witnesses to distant Places; and Matters of Account between Merchant and Merchant and their Factors, great and intricate Questions respecting Insurances, Foreign Bills of Exchange, and other Mercantile Tranlactions arising within a Mercantile City, will often go to Trial by a Jury of the County of Somerset, composed of Persons who (whether such Jury be common or special) mud, necessarily, by their Habits of Life, be unacquainted with the Customs of Merchants, and the Decilions of Courts of Justice in similar Cafes: And that, for thele and many other Reasons, the Petitioners pray the House, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against lb much of the said Bill as affects the County of the City of Brijio/y or that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House to whom the said Bill is re-committed; and the Petitioners are to be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

PRESENT,

The King's Most Excellent MAJESTY in Council.

WHEREAS there was this, Day read at the Board, a Report from a Committee of the Lords of His Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council; viz.

Your Majesty having been pleased, by Your Order in Council of the 26th of this Instant to

refer unto this Committee a Memorial from the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, in the Words following; viz. '

" May it please Your Majesty,

" Having taken into our Consideration the Situation of the Petty Officers, Seamen, Landmen, and Marines, serving on Board Your Majesty's Ships, in respect to the Wages and Proportion of Provisions allowed to them when serving on Board Your Majesty's said Ships; and having consulted some of the most experienced and intelligent Officers in Your Majesty's Naval Service upon thel'e Points, we find they agree in Opinion with us. That, from the great Increase in the Price of every Article of Life, since the prei'ent Rate of Wages was established, it may be for the Advantage of Your Majesty's Service, and an Encouragement to Seamen to enter on Board Your Majesty's Ships, that their Situation be made more comfortable by some Increase to their present Allowance of Wages and Provisions: We do most humbly propose to Your Majesty, That an Addition be made to the W ages of the several Petty Officers, Able Seamen, Ordinary Seamen, Landmen, and Marines, and to the Allowance of Provisions to them, the Officers, and others serving in Your Majesty's Fleet, according to the Plan, and subject to the Regulations hereafter mentioned; viz.

" That an Addition of Five Shillings and Six Pence per Month be made to the present Wages " of the Petty Officers and Able Seamen belonging to Your Majesty's Fleet:

" That an Addition of Four Shillings and Six Pence per Month be made to the Wages of " Ordinary Seamen:

" That an Addition of Three Shillings and Six Pence per Month be made to the Wages of " Landmen:

" That the Allowances, usually called Consolidated Allowances, made to Marines when serving " onShore; viz.To Serjeants, Corporals, and Drummers, at the Rate of Two Pence; and to " Privates, at the Rate of Two Pence Farthing per , be continued to be made to them, when " embarked and serving on Board Your Majesty's Ships:

" That all Petty Officers, Able Seamen, Ordinary Seamen, Landmen, and Marines, who may " hereafter be wounded in Action with the Enemy, do receive the full Amount of their Wages " until their Wounds shall be healed, or until; being declared incurable, they Hull receive a " Pension from the Chest at Chatham, or be admitted into the Royal Hospital at Greenzvich:

"That a Practice which has hitherto prevailed of deducting One Eighth Part of certain Articks of Provisions, as an Indemnification for Leakage or Waste, be discontinued; and that " the full Allowance of Provisions be issued to the Crews of Your Majesty's said Ships, without " any-Deduction whatsoever, on Account of'Leakage or Waste; and that until fiuch Time as this " Regulation can be carried into Effect, Short-allowance Money be paid to the Crews of such " Ships in lieu thereof:

" And lastly,

" That these Regulations should take Place, and be in Force, from the 24th Day of this " Month.

" Which is nevertheless most humbly submitted.

" Spencer.

" Ph. Stephens.

" J. Gambier.

" Admiralty Office, ' " IP- Young."

" 26th April 1797."

The Lords of the Committee, in Obedience to Your Majesty's said Order of Reference, have this Day taken the said Memorial into Consideration; and do agree humbly to report, as their Opinion, to Your Majesty, That they concur in Opinion with the said Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty; and recommend - to Your Majesty to order. That the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, &c. do give Directions to the principal Officers and Commissioners of the Navy, for preparing an Estimate of the Charge of carrying into Execution what is proposed in the said Memorial; and that such Estimate should be laid before Your Majesty in Council.

His Majesty having taken the said Report into Consideration, was pleased, with the Advice of His Privy Council, to approve thereof; and to order, and it is hereby ordered, That the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, &c. do give Directions to the principal Officers and Commissioners of the Navy for preparing an Estimate of the Charge of carrying into Execution what is proposed in the said Memorial, and present the same to His Majesty at this Board.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Befohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties of Six Shillings, and of Eleven Shillings, respectively charged upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrolfcd, printed, or written, any Policy of Insurance for insuring Houses, Furniture, Goods, Wares, Merchandize, or other Property, from Loss by Fire, shall cease and determine.

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty of Three Shillings be charged upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingossed, printed, or written, any Policy of Insurance lor in-luring Houses, Furniture, Goods, Wares Merchandize, or other Property, from Loss by Fire, where the Sum insured thereon shall not amount unto One thousand Pounds, and a Duty of Six Shillings where the Sum insured thereon shall amount unto One thousand Pounds or upwards.

A Petition of the Prisoners (in Number 210) confined for Debt in His Majesty's Gaol of Newgate, _D(:ljlors fc-was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That a considerable Number of the Petitioners have been confined in this Prison, from Three to Four Years, with scarcely any Thing but the Gaol Allowance to subsist upon, to the great Detriment of their Healths, and Ruin of their Families, while the Community laments the loss of many Individuals, who would cheerfully give up their all, if that would satisfy their Creditors, that they might be thereby enabled to purlue their respective Trades and Professions, and, by honed Industry, support themselves and Families, and render that Service to the Public at large that is ex-pefted from them in their Individual Capacity; and that the Petitioners sincerely lament the pro font Situation of Public Affairs, and, as many of them have had the Honour to be at lead useful in the Army and Navy, they feel indignantly their present Thraldom, while their Breads glow with Ardour to be again called forth into Public Service, and, by iignalizing themselves, add fresh Honours to that Country, in Defence of which they would proudly die; and that, without the Interference of the House, the Petitioners have the gloomy Prospect of perpetual Imprisonment before their Eyes; and as this Prison in particular is, at present, to crowded, that there are from 15 to 25 Persons in One Room, comparatively small, consequently they have every Thing to fear from Epidemic Diseases, their dreadful Forerunners, extreme Poverty and Want, having unfortunately too long taken up their Abode in this Place: And therefore imploring the House, to take their distressing same into serious Consideration, and by commilerating their Situation, and that of their Wives and Families, they implicitly rely upon the Humanity that, in all lustances of Distress and Misery, has ever dignified a British House of Commons, ior some Mode ot Relief, under such Regulations and Restrictions, as the Necessity of their same requires, and to the \Y ifdoin and Justice of the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to xMr. Alderman AnJerfon, Mr.

Alderman Combe, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the several Perform, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being respectively Justices of the Peace in and for the County Palatine of Lancaster, Gentlemen, Clergymen, or Freeholders, within the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for obviating and removing Doubts respecting the Holding of the Adjournments of the General Court of Quarter Sessions of the Peace in and for the County Palatine of Lancaster, and for authorizing the Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the said County, to hold an Annual General Sessions, and also a Special Sessions, for the Purposes therein mentioned; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners, being perfectly satisfied with the System adopted by the WHHom of their Ancestors, and still subsisting, for the Dispensation of Justice, and transacting every other Business within the Cognizance and Power of Justices of the Peace, assemblea in Sessions for the said County Palatine, and being fully convinced that long Experience will warrant them in stating such System, when duly attended to and enforced, to be adequate for the Production of every beneficial Purpose, and being at the same Time ferioully apprehen-live, that, should such a Bill be permitted to pass into a Law, very prejudicial Consequences might enfile therefrom; they cannot, without an Abandonment of that fc)uty which they owe to themselves, to their Defendants, and to the Public at large, forbear expressing to Parliament their most pointed Disapprobation of the meditated Change in those Laws and Municipal Insti-tutes which, under the Blessing of Providence, heretofore did, and still might, tend to secure the Happiness, and promote the Prosperity, of so great and opulent a County; and that divers of the Petitioners are resident in the Northern Parts of the County, and in that extensive District known by the Name of which

is separated from the more Southerly Parts by Two large Estuaries, never capable of being traversed, save only at those Times when left dry by the Eflux of the Sea, which Circumstance being the Work of Nature, and peculiar to the Situation of the Petitioners so resident, and who can, by Appeal to the General County Rates, prove that they contribute their full Proportion to ease the Burthens of the County, they do most humbly, but most confidently contend, that the Natural Inconveniencies under which they labour, with Justice cannot, and in Policy ought not, to be augmented by compelling their Attendance at any Courts farther distant than the Town of Lancaster: And therefore, confiding in the Wisdom and Justice of the House, that a System, which has prevailed for more than Four Centuries, may not be set aside by a Mcalure less beneficial to the general Interests of the County, inferring Discredit to those who have heretofore discharged many Parts of the Business which relates to the County at large, and which would be productive of very serious Detriment to the Petitioners and others, pray. That the said Bill may mot pass into a Law; and that they may be heard, by Counsel, against the fame, at the Bar of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of John Palmer, Surveyor and Comptrol- Mr. Palmer' ' ler General of the Poll Office, was presented to the L«ve°topre-House, and read; Setting forth, That in 1782 the fentaPeti-Petitioner, after long Consideration, arranged a Plan tion-to reform the tedious and insecure Method of conveying the Mails through this Kingdom, and make such Improvements therein as to justify an Increase of Postage, and communicated the same to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury; and that various and repeated Objections were made to the Petitioner's Plan by the Pod mailer General and the principal Officers in the Poll Office Establishment, who reported it absolutely impracticable, and prejudicial to the Revenue and Commerce, and declared the old Plan so com-lete that no Alteration was necessary, or, should any e attempted, the Confluences would be fatal to both; and that, after much further Investigation, Labour, and Expence, the Petitioner was enabled to refute the Objections to his Plan, and, being convinced that (notwithstanding the avowed Opposition) it could be made both practicable and beneficial, provided Sufficient Powers were granted him for the Purpose, independent of t he Controul of the Poll Office and his Opponents, he proposed to carry it into Execution on Condition of being allowed Two-and-a-Half per Cent. on all future Increase of the Poll Revenue during his Life, but not a Shilling was to be received if the Undertaking failed; and that the Petitioner on being informed, by the Secretary to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, that his Terms were thought fair, and would be fully complied with if his Plan Succeeded, reited Satisfied with this Arrangement, for no written Contracts are attainable by Individuals employed by G9-vernment; and that in August 1784, being nearly Two Years after the I'irit Communication, nailed in a cons

tinued

586 \6° Mail . A, 1797.

tinued series of Vexations and persevering Opposition, the Petitioner obtained a Trial of his Plan, which succeeded beyond Promise, notwithstanding numerous Impediments, during such Trial, arose from the Poll Office, which called for, and obtained, the most express Interpolation and Protection of the Treasury Board and that a Renewal of Objections and Impediments at the Post Office (topped the Petitioner from extending his Plan till the Summer of 1785, when he was again permitted to proceed, and with such Success as completely to prove it practicable and beneficial; and that the Chancellor of the Exchequer having expressed a wilh to modify the original Agreement, by adding the Produce of the additional Postage to the former Revenue previous to the Commencement of the Petitioner's per Centage on any Increase, and to allow him a Salary of £. 1,500, in lieu of Centage on such additional Postage, your Petitioner acceded to such Modification (though prejudicial to his Interest nearly £. 1,000 a Year); and, in the Autumn of 1785, the Lords of the Treasury ordered a Draft of his Appointment to be made out by their Officers, who, accordingly, prepared a Warrant from the Crown, for appointing the Petitioner Surveyor and Comptroller General during Life, with a general Controul over the Post Office and its Expenditures, and granting him, as well by Way of Reward for his past Services as to encourage him to continue his Exertions, a clear Salary of £. 1,500, together with Two Pounds Ten Shillings per Cent, on the Post Revenue beyond the Amount above specified; and that, on laying the Draft of this intended Appointment before Sir Richard Pepper Arden (then Attorney General) he was of Opinion, that, as the Act of Queen Anne, by which the Post Office was regulated, only provided for Appointments under the Postmaster General, and as the Appointment proposed for the Petitioner was to be for Life, independent of the Postmaster General, a new Act would be requisite; and that the Petitioner hoped the requisite Act would have been obtained, in Confirmation of the Agreement, as he had fully performed his Part, but, after much Anxiety and Suspence, he was given to understand, that, to avoid any Application to Parliament, he mull , take his Appointment under the Postmaster General, which, by the Protection of the Lords of the Treasury, would in EffeCl be made equally efficacious and secure; and that the Petitioner, having, from the first, experienced an avowed Opposition to his Plan from all the Officers in the Post Establishment, was much distressed by the proposed Alteration, but, being unable to compel an Application to Parliament for the Act required, and conceiving it impossible that, while the Benefit of his Rian continued, his specified Profits, or his further Improvements, should be interfered with, he confided in the Faith of his Employers for securing to him the Effect of his Appointment as first proposed, notwithstanding the Deviation in Point of Form, and in the Autumn of 1786 the Lords of the Treasury sent to the Post Office their Warrant for an Appointment under the Postmaster General; and that, in consequence of Changes in the Office of Postmaster General, and other Impediments, the last mentioned Warrant did not fully take Effect till July 1789, and the Petitioner was not enabled to obtain a Shilling towards his Arrears and Expences till October 1786, being Four Years after bringing forward his Plan, and above Two Years after its Commencement; and that the Reports of the Commissioners, appointed by the House to enquire into the State of Public Offices, and the Merits and Claims of the Officers, have given the most decided and honourable Testimony of the Services rendered by the Petitioner to the Public, in reforming Abuses, and greatly increasing the Post Office Revenue; and the Commissioners exprefily declare " the Opposition and Impedi-M ments encountered by the Petitioner to have been

" unprecedented and unmerited and that he was justly {t entitled to the Compensation claimed, being a very " small Part of what his Integrity, Ability, and Zeal, rt had produced, exclusive of the numerous Advantages " accruing to the Public and Commerce, and that, to " secure the Benefit's derived, and to be further ex- pected, from the Petitioner's Plans, it was absolutely " necessary he should be interested in the Productiveness of the whole Post Office Revenue, which might " otherwise fall back into its former State of Delay, " Irregularity, and Confusion, and that some Person, " possessing an Appointment under the Treasury, and " independent of the Post Office, was absolutely necessary to prevent future Abuses and Misconduct " and that, exclusive of the numerous Improvements effected by the Petitioner, and the great Security and Accommodation afforded to Commerce and Travelling, the Post Revenue (which, for Nine Years preceding the Commencement of his Plan, averaged, after a gradual Increase for more than a Century, at only £. 149,333. per Annum, or thereabouts, and was decreasing at the

Rate of £. 13,198. 13 s.per Annum) was in less than Ten Years brought to £.400,000, being an Increase of more than £.250,000 per Annum , and that the Petitioner is assured the Records of the Treasury, from the earliest Period, do not furnish any Instance of a more advantageous Bargain made by that honourable Board for the Public, or one more zealously followed, or more completely fulfilled, on the Part of an Individual; and that the Petitioner, desirous to prosecute, and bring to Perfection, the Plan above-mentioned, upon which Hill many Improvements remain unexecuted, neglected some well-established lucrative private Concerns, in order to devote the Whole of his Time and Attention to the Public Service, and, having made great Sacrifices, undertook, at the Rilk of Ruin to himself and Family, to effeCl a Reform, from which the Public was, without the Possibility of Loss, to (land the Chance of an important and lasting Benefit, subject to a Condition, that the Petitioner should receive (during his Life only) a Fortieth Part of such Benefit as might accrue, and from the progressive Improvement of which, in case of Success, he looked for an Income sufficiently large to permit his realizing a considerable Fortune for his Family, having constantly and openly avowed to Government, from the very Commencement of his Plan, great Expectations as to Profits from its Success, as no Prospect less advantageous could have tempted him to so laborious and hazardous an Undertaking; and that the Petitioner, having incurred the Rilk, and effected the Public Benefit far beyond Promile, naturally hoped his stipulated Reward would have been secured to him, but in this he has been grievously disappointed, for, after experiencing Interruption and Impediments in the ConduCl of his Plan and further Improvements, he was suspended from the Execution of the Duties of his Office, and prevented receiving his specified Share of the increased Revenue, although, according to his Agreement, as modified by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and acceded to by the Petitioner, and the Tenor of his consequent Appointment as originally prepared, he was considered Comptroller General and entitled to his Salary and per Centage for Life, and although, since his Suspension, many of his Plans for further Improvement have been adopted, and the Revenue greatly increased thereby; and that, in lieu of the Petitioner's specified Salary and per Centage, the Lords of the Treasury have thought proper to allow him an Annuity, which (though it may appear considerable in itself) is far short of the Profits arising from his Agreement, and very inadequate to the Purposes for which he adventured in the Undertaking, and, should he be permitted further to extend and improve his Plans, a still further Benefit might be effeCled to the Public Revenue, and ultimately to himself and Family,

TRANSLATION of the Declaration on the Part of their Imperial and Britannick Majesties, signed at , the 16 th of

May 1797.

The Under-signed, in virtue of the Powers with which they have been rumished by their respective Sovereigns, and by their Order, declare as follows:

I.

His Britannick Majesty having made Advances to his Imperial Majesty, amounting in the Whole to the Sum of £. 1,620,000, will cause it to be proposed to

His Parliament, to guarantee a Loan which shall be raised in England for the Service of his Imperial Majesty, on the Terms, and under the Conditions expressed in the Table annexed to this Declaration, and which shall be considered as making a Part of it.

II.

The said Loan shall be for £. 1,620,000 Sterling, and the Produce of it shall be applied exclusively to the Reimbursement of the above-mentioned Advances, and for this Purpose, the Contractors for the Loan shall make the respective Payments due, or to become due, into the Treasury of His Britannick Majesty.

HI.

His Imperial Majesty enters with His Britannick Majesty into a formal Engagement, to pay the Dividends regularly, and Half Yearly, for the Interests, and for the gradual Reimbursement of the said Loan, according to the Conditions of the Table.

IV.

The Fourth and Fifth Articles of the Convention of 1795, relative to the Loan of the said Year 1795, are renewed with respect to the present Loan, and shall have their full and entire Effect in every Thing that regards this Declaration, as if they were expressly inferred therein Word for Word.

V.

His Imperial Majesty will enter, with the Contractors for the present Loan, into the same Engagements, in the same Form, and with the same Advantages and Securities for them, which he entered into in respect to

A. 1797.

the Loan of 1795, by the Oftroi which he published, dated on the 4th of May 1795.

VI.

This Declaration shall be ratified by the respective Sovereigns within Six Weeks, or sooner, if that be possible.

Done at Westminster,this 16 th Day of May 1797.

Signed (L. S.) C. Louis (L. S.) Grenville.

TRANSLATION of the Conditions of the Loan of One Million Six hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling, on Account of his Majesty the Emperor and King.

1. The Loan of One Million Six hundred and

Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling, which shall be raised in London, on Account of his Majesty the Em-

peror and King, shall consist in Bonds, bearing an Interest of Three per Centum per Annum, which shall be signed by MefTrs. Boyd, Benfield, and C°, Bankers to his Imperial Majesty, or by one of the Individuals belonging to the said Firm.

2. A Capital of Three Millions Four hundred and Ninety-three thousand Two hundred and Sixty-one Pounds Nine Shillings, shall be raised by those Bonds; which Sum, at the Rate of Forty -fix and Three-Eighths in Money, for One hundred Pounds Sterling of Capital, makes the above-mentioned Sum of One Million Six hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling.

3. The Lenders shall not be entitled to demand the Redemption of the Stock; but his Imperial Majesty reserves to himself the Power of redeeming it at Par; that is to say, at the Rate of One hundred Pounds Sterling in Money, for One hundred Pounds Sterling of Capital.

4. Although the Redemption of the Capital of

the said Bonds, bearing interest of Three per Cent. shall not be demandable at any Time; his Imperial Majesty engages to remit to the said House of MefTrs. Boyd, Benjeld, and C°, the Annual Sum of Thirty-four

thousand Nine hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings Sterling, by equal Portions, every Three Months j namely, on the First Day of AuguJI, the First Day of November, the First Day of February, and the First Day of May, of every Year, to be applied to the buying up, at the Market Price, of the Capital of the said Bonds, under the Direction of the Commissioners for the buying up of the National Debt of Great Britain, until the Whole of the Capital of the said Bonds shall be entirely extinguished.

5. As a Collateral Security for the said Loan, there shall be deposited in the Hands of the said MefTrs. Boyd, Benfield, and C\ to be by them deposited in the Bank of England, Actions in Mortgage of the Bank of Vienna, for a Sum of Three Millions Four hundred and Ninety-three thousand Two hundred and Sixty-one Pounds Nine Shillings Sterling, the Amount of the Nominal Capital of the said Loan; and according to the gradual Redemption of the Bonds, there shall be withdrawn from the Deposit at the Bank of England, a Quantity of Actions of the Bank of Vienna, proportionate to the Capital of the Bonds which shall have been redeemed.

It is moreover perfectly understood and agreed upon, that not only the aforesaid Annual Sum of Thirty-four thousand Nine hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Two Shillings Sterling, but also the interest arising from the Whole of the Bonds redeemed, shall be employed invariably in the Redemption of the Bonds contrafted

Shaw Lefevre reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Edward Manning, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he scad the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared, by a Promissory Note for .2,500, produced to your Committee, That the said Edward Manning is Holder of the said Note, indorsed to him, for a valuable Consideration.

It also appeared, That the said Note was drawn upon a Paper stamped with an Agreement or Six Shilling Stamp: And,

Mr. John James being examined, said, That the Drawers of the said Note refuse Payment of the fame, and the Person in whose Favour it was drawn, and who indorsed it, is in insolvent Circumstances.

And the Witness further said, That the said zvard Manning, as Indorsee of such Note, brought an Action thereon in His Majesty'-s Court of King's Bench against one of the Drawers, when it was determined, that the said Note, being drawn upon an improper Stamp, ought not to be received in Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Monday Morning next.

That the lame, if passed into a Law, will operate as an immediate Prejudice and Loss to the Petitioners, their ancient Rights and Privileges would be infringed, the various Acts of Parliament passed to lecure the same (as well as those of other ancient Towns in the Kingdom) rendered void, and great Injury would be experienced in the Value of Property, and other local Circumstances: And therefore praying, That so much, and such Parts, of the said Bill, as authorizes the Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the said County, to hold the said several Annual General Sessions and the Special Sessions therein mentioned at may

not pass into a Law'.

Pfririon from A Petition and Representation of the there-under Tinwln-" written Gentlemen and Farmers, being Owners and shire rei|«.&- Occupiers of Land, in the County of Lincoln, was Prfcc o/corn. Patented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Sic. ' the Petitioners, relying on the Regulations which were

established by the Legislature, respecting the Importation of Corn, in the Thirty-first Year of His Majesty's Reign, have, at a very considerable Expence, cultivated a large Quantity of Land for the Production of Corn, the Price of which is now so extremely depressed as not to coinpenfate for the Charge of railing the fame, and, as that Deprellion has been occasioned by continuing to allow the free Importation of Corn, contrary to those Regulations, long after all actual Scarcity, and all Apprehension thereof, had cealed, the Petitioners conceive themselves to be materially injured, more particularly at a Time when the Charges of cultivating Land are so greatly augmented by a vast Increase of Parochial and County Rates, and by raising Men for the Navy, Army, and Militia, in which Services so many Labourers are engaged, that the Price of Labour is advanced very far beyond all former Experience, upwards of Eight Shillings Day having been commonly paid during a great Part of the lait Harvest; and although the Petitioners lament the Necessity of supporting l'uch extensive Services, as the unavoidable Consequence of War, yet they are fully convinced that it is the sincere Wilh of our Gracious Sovereign to put an End to the Calamities attending it, and that such Measures will be pursued, under His Authority, as may moll speedily conduce to a safe and honourable Peace; an Event ardently to be wished for, and which the Petitioners will not, on their Part, obstruct and retard by any ill advised Interference with the Executive Government in its Endeavours to accomplish that moll important Object and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, that a very considerable Quantity of Corn is now in Possession of the Growers, by reason of the Impofiibility of disposing of it, except at a great Lois, on which Account much will probably remain for lbme Time unthrdhed: They have also Reason to believe, that very many Peffons, availing themselves of the low Price, have laid up a considerable Quantity of Corn for future Use j and, as the Fields at present 9

have the most promising Appearance, there is Reason to apprehend that the Price of Corn will be further deprelled, should the free Importation of Foreign Com be longer permitted, contrary to those Regulations,; and the Petitioners conceive that Corn of every Sort, amply sufficient for the Consumption of the whole Kingdom, w'ould be grown within it, if Regulations, equally tending to prevent too high or too low a Price, were established, not to be departed from, except in Cafes of Necessity, and then only so long as the Ne-celfity should exist; but, if Persons, cultivating Land at a large Expence, shall have but a very uncertain Prospect of Compensation for the Charge and Rilk of producing Corn, by Reason of any unnecessary Departure from such established Regulations, in l'uch a same Agriculture will be checked, the Cultivation of our Waite Lanctedil'couraged, and we mult depend for Support on the Produce of other States, enriching them, and promoting their Tillage, to the great Dil-couragement of our own: Thus becoming dependent on others, we should occasionally fuller most severely from that very Scarcity against which it is intended to provide: And the Petitioners further represent, that a Petition to the House, agreed to at a certain Meeting, held at Bojloti on the 29th Day of March lait (at which Meeting John Cartwright, Esquire, was Chairman) did not (as the Petitioners verily believe) cx-press the real Sentiments of the Inhabitants in general of that Town and Neighbourhood, nor of the Freeholders, nor of the taxed Householders, but only the Sentiments of a very i'rnall Number of Persons of any of those Descriptions, so far as relates to the Election of Members of the House; and that the Petitioners are convinced, that a Reform of such Election, extending -the Right of Suffrage either univerlally or to every taxed Householder, would tend clircdrily and unavoidably to the Subveriion of our present Constitution: And therefore praying the House will take these several Matters into Consideration, and do therein as to their Judgment shall i'eem most fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, Petition from of the City of Exeter, in Chamber assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the gulatethe Bill to regulate the Trial of Causes and Indictments which arise within the Limits of certain Cities and Towns Corporate within this Kingdom; and Setting forth, That, if the Change proposed by the said Bill for the Administration of Justice, within the City and County of Exeter, in criminal or civil Cafes, should take place, the same would be an Infringement on the Rights of the Petitioners, and would be attended with great Inconvenience and additional Expence to the Inhabitants of the said City: And therefore praying.

That the City and County of the City of Exeter may be exempted from the Provisions of the said Bill; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against so much of tiic said Bill as aflefts the Rights of the Petitioners, and the said City.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House to whom the said Bill is re-committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Decision. of the Court of King's Bench, and as the Law now Hands, the Owners and Masters of Ships are held to be responhble to the Owners of their respective Cargoes, for all Damages which may happen to their Cargoes, that do not arise by the Act of God immediately operating on the Vessel; that from this Interpretation of the Law, the Owners and Masters of Ships are answerable for the Loss or Damage which has happened, or may happen, to the Cargoes of their respective Vessels, by numerous Accidents, which it is impossible for them either to foresee or prevent; and that this Responsibility was totally unknown, both to the Owners and Masters of Ships, and to the Owners of the Cargoes, until the above-mentioned Decision: And the Witness added, That unless the Owners and Masters of Ships are relieved from such Responfibi-

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS, upon the Representatiort of Our Lords Commissioners of Our Admiralty respecting the Proceedings of the Seamen and Marines on board certain of Our Ships at The Nore, We were pleased to command Our laid Lords Commissioners of Our Admiralty to signify to the said Seamen and Marines Out gracious Intentions, expressed in Our Royal Declaration, under Our Sign Manual, bearing Date at ' James's, the Twenty-seventh Day of May Instant, in the Words following: " Whereas it has been reprefented unto Us, That, notwithstanding the Declarations made in Our Name, and by Our Authority, by " Our Lords Commissioners of Our Admiralty, of Our gracious Intentions to recommend to the Consideration of Parliament, to augment the Wages and Allowances of the Seamen and Marines of Our Fleet, " which Our gracions Intentions and Declarations have since been carried into Effect by an Act of Parliament; and, notwithstanding the Communication made by Our Right Trusty and Right Well-beloved " Cousin and Councillor Richard Earl Hozue, Admiral of Our Fleet, ot Our gracious Intentions towards " the Seamen and Marines of Our Fleet, for the Pardon of the Offences by them committed, and Our Royal Proclamation thereupon, bearing Date the Eleventh Day of May Instant; and notwithstanding " the Sentiments of Duty and Gratitude, with which the same were received by the Seamen and Marines " of Our other Squadrons, yet the Crews on board certain of Our Ships at The Nore, have not only since the full Manifestation of all these Our gracious Intentions and Declarations been guilty of clivers Acts of " Mutiny and Disobedience of Orders, but have even proceeded to other Acts of the raoft heinous and trea-

sonable Nature, by firing upon some of Our Ships in order to compel them to submit to their Direction; " have threatened and taken Measures for Hopping the Commerce of the Kingdom passing to and from the Port of London, and have, by Terror of their Force, compelled Two Frigates to desist from executing a " particular Service, which by Our Orders they were directed to perform: We, thinking it right to warn

" all Our Seamen and Marines on board the said Ships, of the heinous Nature of the Offences by them " committed, and of the dangerous Consequences thereof to the Spirit and Discipline of the Navy,

" and to the Welfare of their Country, as well as to their own Safety, do hereby earnestly require and enjoin " all Our said Seamen and Marines, immediately on the Notification of this Our Royal Declaration, to " return to the regular Discharge of their Duty, as has already been done by the Crews of Our other Squadrons and Fleets, Rationed at Porlfmonth and Plymouth, and elsewhere: And whereas We are well assured " that a great Part of the Seamen and Marines on board the said Ships at The Nore, abhor and deteft the " Criminal Proceedings which are still persisted in on board the said Ships, and are defircus to return to their " Duty: Now, We being desirous to extend Our Gracious Intentions of Pardon, to all such Seamen and " Marines so lcrving on board Our said Ships at The Nore who may have returned, or shall return, upon " the Notification of this Our Royal Declaration, to the regular and ordinary Discharge of their Duty, " have authorized, and do hereby authorize and empower Our said Lord Commissioners of Our Admiralty, " or any Three of them, to signify to all such Seamen and Marines, who may have been guilty of any of the " treasonable Acts aforesaid, or of any Mutiny or Disobedience of Orders or Neglect of Duty, and who " have returned, or who shall, upon Notification hereof, on board their respective Ships, return to the " regular and ordinary Discharge of their Duty, Our Royal Intentions to grant to all such Seamen and " Marines Our most Gracious Pardon, and to promise, in Our Name, to all such Seamen and Marines, " who have so returned, or shall so return to the regular and ordinary Discharge of their Duty, Our moll " gracious Pardon accordingly: And We do hereby declare. That all such Seamen and Marines, who shall " have so returned, or shall so return to their Duty, and to whom the said Lords Commissioners of Our " Admiralty, or any Three of them, shall so promise Our Pardon, shall receive the same accordingly, and " shall be discharged and released from all Prosecutions, Imprisonments, and Penalties incurred by reason " of any of the Acts aforesaid, or by reason of any Act of Mutiny or Disobedience of Orders, or any Breach " or Neglect of Duty previously committed by them or any of them; hereby declaring at the same Time, " that all such Seamen and Marines who shall not take the Benefit of this Our gracious Pardon, shall from " henceforth be considered as liable, according to the Nature of their Offences, to such Punishment as the " Articles of War and the Law have provided for the fame." And whereas Our Right Trusty and Right Vol. 52. 7 X Well-

630 i 0 JunA. 1797.

Well-beloved Cousin and Councillor George John Earl Spencer, Our Tiufiy and Well-beloved Charles George Lord Arden of Our Kingdom of Ireland, and William Young, Esquire, Rear Admiral of the White, being Three of the Lords Commissioners of Our Admiralty, did cause Our gracious Intentions expressed in such

- Our Declaration, to be signiiied to the Crews of Our Ships at The A and did require such Crews to

return to their due Obedience accordingly: And whereas it has been represented to Us, that some of the

Crews of Our said Ships have been delirous of returning to their Obedience accordingly, but have been

- prevented from lb doing by Violence; and others of Our Ships, in the attual Discharge of their Duty, have been fired upon, and Attempts have been made to prevent some of Our Ships from proceeding according to the Orders of their Commanders: And whereas such continued Perseverance in rebellious and treasonable Attempts against Our Crown and Dignity, after repeated Admonitions and Offers of Our gracious Pardon, render it necessary fqr Us to call on all Our loving-Subjects to be aiding and assisting in repressing the fame;

We have thought fit, by the Advice cf Our Privy Council, to issue this Our Royal Proclamation, and We do

- hereby strictly enjoin and command all Our Admirals, Generals, Commanders, and Officers of Our Forces

by Sea and Land, and all Magistrates whatsoever, and all others Our loving Subjects, that they in their several Stations do use their utmost Endeavours, according to Law, to supprels all such mutinous and treasonable Proceedings, and to use all lawful Means to bring the Persons concerned therein, their Aiders and Abettors, to Justice: And YVe.do hereby strictly enjoin and command all Our loving Subjects whatsoever

not to give any Aid, Comfort, Assistance, or Encouragement whatsoever to any Person or Persons concerned in "any such mutinous and treasonable Proceedings, as they wall answer the same at their Peril; and also, to the utmost of their Power and according to Law, to prevent all other Persons from giving any such Aid, Assistance, Comfort, or Encouragement. — Given at Our Court at St. James's the Thirty-first Day of May One thousand l'even hundred and ninety-seven, and in the Thirty-seventh Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the KING.

Ordered, That the said Proclamation do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

RcfolvedJ % That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Contributor to the Loan of Eighteen Millions, granted by an Act of this Session of Parliament, who shall, within a Time to be limited, produce at the Bank of England the Receipts for the Sums by them reflectively subscribed, or shall be possessed of Capital Stock created on Account of the said Loan of Eighteen Millions, not exceeding the Amount of their original Subscription, shall be entitled to an Annuity of Seven Shillings and Six Pence for every One Hundred Pounds subscribed, to commence from the 5th Day of April 1797, and to continue for the Term of Sixty-two Years and Nine Months, and then to ccafe, which said Annuity shall be added to, and made One Joint Stock with, certain Annuities, payable at the 'Bank of England, which were granted for the several Terms of Ninety-nine, Ninety-eight, Eighty, Seventy-eight, Seventy-seven Years, Seventy-five Years and an Half, Sixty-nine Years and a Quarter, Sixty-six Years and a Quarter, Sixty-five Years and a Quarter, and Sixty-four Years and a Quarter, and were,.by the Acts of the Fourth, Twentieth, and Twenty-second Years of His present Majesty, and by several subsequent Acts, consolidated and made One Joint Stock of Annuities, and shall be payable, paid, and transferrable, at the same Time, and in the same Manner, as the Laid Annuities so consolidated by the Acts of the Fourth, Twentieth, and Twenty-second Years of His present Majesty, are payable and tran.'tcrrable at the Bank of England.

Erf ok 'cJ, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provisions of an Act, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, so far as the same relate to the Limits particularly described therein as the Limits to be observed between the Lowlands and Highlands of Scotland, shall be discontinued 3

from the 5th Day of July 1797, and other Provisions be made for the Purpose of narrowing the Limits of the Districts described as the Highlands of Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Duties granted by several Acts of the Thirty-third, Thirty-fifth, and Thirty-seventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, on the Cubical Content of Stills used or employed lor the making or distilling of Low Wines or Spirits from Corn, Crain, Mait, Tilts, Cyder, or Perry, or other Walk or Liquor made on, brewed from any Sort of Brit ft Materials, or any Mixture therewith, and on Licences for retailing Aquavits, shall be extended to all such Parts or Places in Scotland as shall not be within the Limits to be provided as the Limits of the Highlands of Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Licence Duties, granted by several Acts of the Thirty-third and Thirty-fifth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, on the Content of Stills used for the distil ling of Spirits from the Barley, Beer, or Bigg, of the Growth of the Highlands of Scotland, shall be discontinued as to all such Parts and Places in Scotland as shall not be within the Limits to be provided as the Limits of the Highlands of Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Annual Duty of Four Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Content of every Still which shall have been used or employed in distilling and drawing off Spirits from the Barley, Beer, or Bigg, of the Growth of the Highlands of Scotland) at any Time on or after the ift Day of December 1796, and which shall continue to be so used and employed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exemption from the Duty on Malt, granted by Two Acts passed in the Thirty-third and Thirty-fifth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for all Malt used in extracting Spirits within the Highlands ol Scotland) should ccafe and determine.

A Petition of Alexander Champion, Junior, Robert Livie, John Roberts, Henry and William Bell,

was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for authorizing the Commissioners of the Stamp Duties to direct the Note therein mentioned to be marked or stamped with a proper Stamp, upon Payment of the Duty in that Behalf; and Setting forth. That, if the said Bill should pal's into a Law, the Petitioners conceive it will be very injurious to their Interests: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Leeds:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House That the Lords do concur in the Resolutions, communicated to them at a Conference on Monday the First of May last, on the Subject of providing more effectual Means for promulgating the Statutes of this Realm, and have agreed to an Address to be presented to His Majesty thereupon; to which Address the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Resolved, That this House will fend an Answer to that Part of the said Message which relates to the said Address by MeftTengers of their own.-

And then the Messengers again withdrew.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said merft Gracious Message be now taken into Consideration.

Conjuncture, to provide for the Public Security: With this View we shall proceed, without Delay, in pursuance of the Recommendation of His Majesty, to consider of such further Provision as it may be necctlary to make for the more effectual Prevention and Punishment of all traitorous Attempts to excite Mutiny in any Part of His Majesty's- Forces, or to withdraw them from their Duty and Allegiance, and from that Obedience and Discipline which are so important to the Prosperity and the Safety of the British Empire:

That we have the fulled Reliance, that all His Majesty's faithful Subjects, from Sentiments of Loyalty and Attachment to His Majesty, and a just Anxiety for their dearest Interests, will be eager to manifest, at so important a Crisis, a full Determination to contribute, on every Occaficft, their utmost Exertions for the Support of legal Authority, the Maintenance of Peace and Order, and the general Protection and Defence of His Majesty's Kingdoms.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Petition from thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, Lessees, and La?yuayf Wharfingers, of certain Quays upon the River 'Thames, again It Lon-in the Port and City of London, known by the Name and Appellation of The Legal Quays, and of certain c' Warehouses situated thereon, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation, and Security, of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth. That the said Quays were established and legalized by Acts of Parliament in the Reigns of Queen Elizabeth and King Charles the Second, and by virtue of certain Royal Commissions, proceeding under the Sanction and Authority of those Acts: And that the said Quays, and the Warehouses situated thereon, are of great Value to the Petitioners, many of whom depend entirely upon the Rents thereof, or the Biifiness transacted at them, for the Support of themselves and Families, and they mull, in many Instances, be brought to Poverty and Ruin, and in all Instances very severely injured, if the Business which has been carried on there should be removed to any other Place; and that, if the said Bill should pals into a Law, the necessary Consequence will be, the Removal of the Trade, either wholly, or in a great Degree, from the said Quays and Warehouses of the Petitioners, and the Places where it has heretofore been carried on under the Authority aforesaid, to other Places remote from the said Quays; and that, the Petitioners Ancestors and Predecessors, and they themselves, have, from Time to Time, laid out large Sums of Money upon the said Quays, and in erecting and improving the said Warehouses, in the just and reasonable Expectation that the Trade of the City of London would continue to be carried on as heretofore; and that the Petitioners have at all Times used their utmost Endeavours to render the said Quays and Warehouses commodious to the Merchants of the City of London, and to the Persons appointed to conduct and manage the Affairs of the Revenue within the Port of London; and that the said Property, thus established by Law, has become at divers Times, and is now, the Subject of Family Settlements, and other Securities; and that the Petitioners can only be rendered secure of a Compensation for the Loss of their present legal Rights and Interests, by a full, sufficient, and adequate Fund being set apart for their Indemnity, by proper Provisions in the said Bill: And therefore praying.

That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel,

Agent?, and Witness'es, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them; and that Provision may be made therein for indemnifying the Petitioners, and all other Persons, being Owners of, or interested in, the Legal Quays and Warehouses aforesaid, for all such Lois, Damage, and Injury, as they may sustain from the Operation and Consequences of the said Bill, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witness'es, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Copy, of the Resolutions of the Court of Directors of the Bank of England, on the 13th June 1797.

And the said Paper was also read.

The said Paper is as followeth;

RESOLUTIONS of the Court of Directors of the Bank of on the 13th 1797.

At a Court of Directors at the Bank, on Tuesday, the 13th June 1797.

THE Governor laid before the Court the following LETTER from the Chancellor of the

Exchequer; viz.

m . Downing Street, June 12th 1797.

" Gentlemen,

On a Consideration of the Particulars which you have communicated to me, respecting the State of the Calli and Bullion in the Bank, and the Alteration which has taken place since the Order of the 26th ' February, I feel strongly impressed with an Opinion, that it would not be for the Public Interest, or for that of the Bank, under all Circumstances, that the Bank should re-commence Payments in Calli, at the Period when the Act passed this Session would expire. I therefore think it my Duty to request you to Hate to your Court, that unless I should receive any further Communication from them which might tend to change this Opinion, it is my Intention, on an early Day, to move for Leave to bring in a Bill to prolong the Prohibition now subsisting.

I have the Honour to be,

Gentlemen,

Gov' and DepT Govr Youf obedient humble Servant,

Resolved,

That this Court do assent to the Measure proposed in the Chancellor of the Exchequer's Letter, for prolonging the Prohibition, now subsisting, of paying in Specie, which, under the present Circumstances of the Country, appears to the Court expedient to be continued for a limited Time; but it may be adviseable that a Power should be reserved to Ihorten the Time, and enable the Bank to renew its Payments in Cash, in such Manner, and under such Authority, as shall be judged proper.

Resolved,

That the Governor and Deputy Governor do wait' on the Chancellor of the Exchequer this Day, with the above Resolution.

v.'.r. and read; 'Tiling Notice of the said Bill; and Setti: g ! -: rV, I hat the Petitioners beg Leave to reprelent to the 1 h u e, that, under Pretence of improving the Lands in the ia:J Pa;i!h, the Cottagers, and other Persons entits-d to Light of Common on the Lands intended to be in ha. 1, wilt be deprived of an inestimable Privilege, which they now enjoy, of turning a certain Number of their Cows, Calves, and Sheep, on and over the said Lands; a Privilege that enables them not only to maintain themselves and their Families in the Depth of Winter, when they cannot, even for their Money, obtain from the Occupiers of other Lands the smallest Portion of Milk or Whey for such necessary Purpose, but, in Addition to this, they can now supply the Grazier with young or lean Stock at a reasonable Price, to fatten and bring to Market at a more moderate Rate for general Consumption, which they conceive to be the most rational and etleftual Way of establishing Public Plenty and Cheapncfs of Provision; and they further conceive, that a more ruinous Eiieft of this Inclosure will be the almost total Depopulation of their Town, now filled with bold and hardy Husbandmen, from among whom, and the Inhabitants of other open Parillies, the Nation has hitherto derived its greatest Strength and Glory, in the Supply of its Fleets and Armies, and driving them, from Necessity and Want of Employ, in vast Crowds, into manufacturing Towns, where the very Nature of their Employment, over the Loom or the Forge, soon may walle their Strength, and consequently debilitate their Pof-tcrity, and by imperceptible Degrees obliterate that great Principle of Obedience to the Laws of God and their Country, which forms the Character of the simple and artless Villagers, more equally distributed through the Open Countries, and on which so much depends the good Order and Government of the State; Thele are ibme of the Injuries to themselves as Individuals, and of the ill Confecyucnces to the Public, which the Petitioners conceive will follow from this, as they have already done from many Inclosures, but which they did not think they were entitled to lay before the House (the Constitutional Patron and Protector of the Poor) until it unhappily came to their own Lot to be exposed to them through the Bill now pending: And therefore praying the House to take their Petition into serious Consideration, and that the said Bill may not be buffered to proceed to a Second Reading.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Dairy Men and Butter Factors, or Dealers in Butter, in the County of Norfolk, for and on the Behalf of themselves, and the several other Dairy Men and Butter Factors, or Dealers in Butter, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prevent Abuses and Frauds in the Packing, " Weight, and Sale, of Butter, and to repeal certain " Acts relating the reto}" and Setting forth, That a very considerable Quantity of Butter is made in the said County, and that any Circumstances which might induce the Farmers or Dairy Men to lessen the Number of their Cows would eventually prove extremely prejudicial to the Interests of the Nation at large, as it would, in a very material Degree, tend to reduce the Number of Cattle and Swine reared in the said County, and forwarded from thence to the London and other-Markets; and that the Petitioners are perfectly willing to admit the Necessity of every Man being compelled to deliver every Tub, Firkin, or Half Firj kin, of Butter, of its proper Weight, and that the Quality should be as good as the Nature of Things will admit} but that, although the Butter may be of its full Weight when sent, the Heat of Weather, and Length of Time it is necessarily upon the Road, will frequently occasion a Diminution in the Weight thereof} and that there are certain Times and Seasons of the Year, and other Circumstances, in which it is totally inipoffible so to manufacture Butter that it should reach London in good Condition} and that the Ends of Justice and Equity would be much more fully answered if the Magistrates, acting for each Division, District, or Riding, were to appoint proper Persons to weigh and inspect the Butter previous to its being sent from the Country to the London Market, than by Adoption of the Plan now proposed: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard against the same by themselves or their Counsel.

A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Dairy Men and Farmers in the Neighbourhood of Malton, in the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read} likewise taking Notice of the said Bill -, and Setting forth, That, if the same should pass into a Law in its present Form, and, if certain Clauses in the said former Act (for the Repeal or Alteration of which no Provision is made by the said Bill) should continue unrepealed and unaltered, the Petitioners conceive that the Provisions of the said Bill and Act would be oppressive to themselves, would considerably injure the Sale and Exportation of Butter to the Metropolis, and tend to lessen the Number of Dairy Farms in Yorkshire, which are materially supported by

such Sale and Exportation: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, or Agent, against such Parts of the said Bill as are of Public Inutility, and prejudicial to their own Interests, and also may be allowed to submit to the Consideration of the House such Alterations and Amendments, in the said Act, as may tend to prevent or remove the Injuries and Inconveniencies complained of by the Petitioners} that the said Bill may not pass into

Juniu 797.

a Law as it how Hands } and that the Petitioners may , have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet. r

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is re-committed} and the Petitioners are to be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Charles EUis being examined, said, That the Com-iniilioners for the Affairs of Taxes were, previous to the Year 1787, constantly rated to the Land Tax, for 'I heir Salaries and the Profits of their Offices, within the District called Offices executed in Westminster within the City and Liberty of Westminster: That the Office of the said Commissioners was, in 1787, removed to Somerset Place, within the Duchy Liberty

in the Strand, in the County of Middlesex;_and since

liich Removal, the said Commissioners have been af-ll fil'd to the Land Tax, as well within the said Dif-tlilt called Offices executed in Hall, as

within the District of the Duchy Liberty, Doubts having arisen, whether, in respect to the Nature of the Duties of their Office, they ought not to be considered as Officers of the Exchequer, and, consequently, as Officers within Westminster Hall:

And the Witness further said. That in order to accommodate the Difference between the said Dif-trifts, it has been agreed to make the Assessment upon the said Commissioners and their Officers in the said District for Offices executed in Westminster Hall, and to pay One-third of the Sum affeifl'ed to the Collectors of the Land Tax, for the said Duchy Liberty in Aid of the Assessment thereon.

A Petition of Thomas Macklin of Fleet Street, in Petit ion of Mr. the City of London, Printfeller, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner fenta hath, at a very considerable Expence, promoted and ££f1,eof establillied various Works, which have for several nns Years past given great Encouragement to the Artists in Painting and Engraving, and thereby raised the Celebrity of the English School; and that the depressed State of the Arts induced the Petitioner to form other Plans for their Encouragement, but, upon examining the State of his Relources, he found it utterly im-pradicable to prosecute such new Designs without converting into Money Part of his Stock, and therefore he determined to solicit the Aid of Parliament, to enable him to dispose of his Collection of Modem Paintings, in order to prevent the heavy Loss which would unavoidably be sustained by a Sale of the same in the common Way: But the Petitioner was not sufficiently apprized of that State of the Arts, or of his own Resources, on which the Necessity or Propriety of an Application to Parliament mult depend, and on which the Relief prayed for mull be founded, until the Time for presenting Private Petitions during the present Session of Parliament had elapsed; and that a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the Purpose aforesaid hath been prepared, and is now ready to be presented to the House: And, forasmuch as it is highly important to the Petitioner that the Object of such intended Bill should be ac-. complished with as little Delay as possible, he therefore prays, That the House will give Leave to present his aforesaid Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable him to dispose of the said Modern Paintings by Way of Chance, without incurring any Penalties, notwithstanding the Time limited for presenting limilar Petitions during the present Session is elapsed.

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Benjamin tFeJl, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Petitioner hath, at a very considerable Expence, promoted and established various Works, which have for several Years past given great Encouragement to the Artists in Painting and Engraving, and thereby raised the Celebrity of the English School, to a greater Degree of Per-

section than was known in this Country before, particularly in Historical Painting and Engraving: That the Petitioner is desirous to bring forward other Productions of a similar Nature, which may further tend to promote and encourage those Arts, and lead them to a (till greater State of Perfection; but cannot enter into any new Engagements or Undertakings, until his present Collection of Modern Paintings is disposed of: And the V *

Witness added, That unless some Encouragement is . given by Parliament, to enable the Petitioner to dispose of the said Collection to the belt Advantage, there must be a very great Loss in the disposing thereof by the common Mode of Sale.

John Opie and William Hamilton, Esquires, confirmed the above Evidence.
